articles.text:
Sunday, September 20th 2026
	
	
		
	
	
This Week in Gaming (Week 39)
As we enter the last full week of September, we kick off with a sequel AAA release from a Finnish developer that has many famous games in its catalogue. If that's not for you, then how about a racing game unlike any other racing game you've seen or maybe you prefer to manage a graveyard? We also have some slow cruising and a horror spin-off from a franchise that started back in 1999, as well as the option to be a wild west pioneer, hopefully without dysentery on the trail. Don't forget to check out some of the other games launching this week as well.
Control Resonant / This week's AAA release / Thursday 24 September
After years in confinement at the hands of the Federal Bureau of Control (FBC), Dylan Faden emerges into a warped Manhattan at the peak of a paranatural crisis. Charged with combating a mysterious cosmic entity as it alters fundamental aspects of our reality, Dylan must harness his new-found powers to take the fight to the myriad threats overwhelming Manhattan. Steam linkHappy Wheels / Monday 21 September
Happy Wheels is a side-scrolling, physics-based, community driven sandbox game, now (finally) available, ad-free, on Steam. Select your inadequately prepared racer, and disregard severe consequences in your desperate pursuit of short-lived victory. Choose from more than 5 million user created levels or create and share your own. Steam linkGraveyard Keeper 2 / Demo available / Tuesday 22 September
The most inaccurate medieval cemetery sim is back! Restore The Town, manage the graveyard, automate production, lead your undead army into battle and turn the zombie problem into a thriving business! Graveyard Keeper 2 is the grotesque sequel that's deeper than six feet, and more unhinged than ever. Steam linkSlow Roads / Demo available / Wednesday 23 September
Slow Roads is a casual driving game designed to capture the zen of a long drive on a scenic road. Zone out as you coast along lifelike roads that wind endlessly through procedurally-generated landscapes, with configurable locations, road styles, seasons, weather, and vehicles. Generate a unique world, throw on some music, and just drive. Steam linkSilent Hill: Townfall / Thursday 24 September
Returning to an island town to 'put things right', Simon Ordell descends into a world of tense evasion, explosive confrontations, and mind-bending puzzles that slowly surface the truth of St. Amelia. Steam linkWild West Pioneers / Early access / Friday 25 September
Wild West Pioneers is a city-builder adventure about leading settlers into the untamed frontier. Build and manage growing settlements, establish production chains, and explore the world. Follow a story of gold rush dreams, dangerous encounters, and the search for your family. articles.title: Noctua fans prevent the CAIM1 ‘Anti-AI’ 4K camera from throttling — unusual camera’s processor gets toasty as it records while performing cryptographic calculations
articles.text:
Noctua fans prevent the CAIM1 ‘Anti-AI’ 4K camera from throttling — unusual camera’s processor gets toasty as it records while performing cryptographic calculations
Noctua says it is 'cooling a camera built to prove reality.'
A premium PC DIY fan brand has announced that one of its prized spinners is being used in a 4K camera. Noctua says that its NF-A4x10 5V PWM was used by the CAIM1 camera designers due to its quiet, compact nature and strong airflow and pressure performance. This camera runs two intensive processing tasks simultaneously within a compact shell, high-bitrate imaging and cryptography, hence the need for active cooling to prevent throttling.
The CAIM1 is something of a niche product. It has been designed to create photo and video captures that one can say with certainty haven’t been altered or generated using AI. Noctua says it is “cooling a camera built to prove reality.” CAIM1 is short for Counter Artificial Intelligence Machine 1.
From the brief description provided by the source, this anti-AI functionality seems to work by piping the imagery directly from the lens/sensor through an “onboard hardware attestation with edge cryptographic proof generation” process. This is stored on the camera’s “immutable, decentralized storage, enabling the origin of the media to be verified independently,” says the Austrian air-cooling specialist.
Of course Noctua’s involvement was beneficial to the camera makers for its high-quality precision fans. The CAIM1 generates heat through its high-bitrate 4K imaging activity, its cryptographic processing, all within the confines of a compact handling-friendly shell. Other key considerations of the designers were precise PWM fan control, and finding a fan with minimal noise (as the camera records audio) and minimal microvibrations.
Noctua says its NF-A4x10 5V, with its PWM’s SSO2 bearing system and smooth motor drive fitted the bill. This tiny fan was leveraged in a unified single-airstream cooling design with custom anti-vibration mounts, situated right behind the image sensor. This directs air across the sensor’s alloy heatsink backplate, and which gets exhausted though the camera chassis left side.
Our nozzle-headed readers will also be pondering over the Prusa branding on the camera body. The simple answer is that the CAIM1 is still at the prototyping stage and these models have been prepared using 3D printers and Prusament PETG Noctua Beige and Noctua Brown for the outer shell and fan mount. CAIM1 devices will be showcased at a handful of trade shows in Japan later this month. However, commercial batches are targeting Q1 2027 availability.

articles.title: SEMICON India 2026 concludes with 15 announcements, headlined by Indian startups and student teams
articles.text:
SEMICON India 2026 concludes with 15 announcements, headlined by Indian startups and student teams
The final day put the spotlight on Indian startups and student teams building on homegrown chip platforms, alongside a new industry report projecting sharp growth for the country's semiconductor market.
New Delhi's Yashobhoomi convention centre wrapped up SEMICON India 2026 on September 19, 2026 with a concluding session that packed in 15 announcements, ranging from indigenous processor challenges to sovereign computing partnerships and skilling tie-ups, according to a press release from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
The day put the spotlight on Indian startups and student teams building on homegrown chip platforms, alongside a new industry report projecting sharp growth for the country's semiconductor market.
SEMICON India 2026, the fifth edition of the event, ran from September 17 to 19 and was jointly organised by the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) and SEMI on the theme 'Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem'.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the conference on its opening day. The event has grown into one of the country's largest semiconductor gatherings, bringing together government bodies, global chipmakers, academic institutions and start-ups as India works to build out design, manufacturing and packaging capabilities under its broader Semicon India programme.
Student teams turn indigenous chips into real products
The clearest entrepreneurial story from the closing session came from the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) Grand Challenge, organised by Maker Village under the Chips to Startup Programme of MeitY. The contest drew 1,236 teams comprising 5,045 participants, and three winning teams shared a total prize purse of Rs 60 lakh.
Meevisai Technologies, representing a SASTRA University team, took the first prize for an autonomous water-surface cleaning robot built on the indigenous SHAKTI processor developed by IIT Madras, aimed at cleaning ponds and temple tanks. Digiscope LLP won the second prize for VEGA Chikitsa, a digital stethoscope that captures heart and lung sounds with real-time filtering and machine-learning-assisted murmur screening, built on CDAC's VEGA processor. Zetawave Technologies, an IISc Bengaluru team, took the third prize for a forest-environment monitoring system, also on the VEGA platform.
Startups get investor time, and the market outlook brightens
Startup engagement ran through several other parts of the day. Under Startup Mitra, 11 startups pitched to more than 20 venture capital investors, with Elphins Technologies placing first, Meukron Technologies second, and Multi Nano Sense Technologies and CraftifAI sharing third place. A parallel SEMICON India Hackathon drew 3,808 team registrations from 881 colleges and 1,053 ideas, with 10 teams reaching the grand finale; teams from VIT Vellore and IIT Madras emerged as winners.
Adding context to the day's numbers, EY and the India Semiconductor and Electronics Association launched a report titled 'Semicon India 2.0: From Capacity Creation to Ecosystem Leadership'. The report estimates that India's semiconductor market could grow from nearly $64 billion in 2026 to $200 billion by 2035, and it lays out a roadmap for converting domestic demand and design talent into leadership across manufacturing, advanced packaging and innovation, reports suggest. Beyond the startup track, the session also saw C-DAC launch PARAM Vidya, a plug-and-play AI lab-in-a-box for universities and MSMEs, and PARAM Shavak-QS, a compact quantum simulation platform, alongside partnerships between C-DAC and NLC India, and C-DAC and Bharat Electronics Limited, for sovereign data-centre and computing infrastructure.
What is RISC-V and why India is betting on it
RISC-V is an open, royalty-free processor architecture, meaning any company or research group can design chips on it without paying licensing fees to a proprietary chip-design firm. For India, which has historically depended on foreign architectures for processor design, this matters because it lowers the barrier for home-grown players to build their own chips from the ground up.
That is why platforms like SHAKTI, developed at IIT Madras, and VEGA, developed by CDAC, carry weight beyond the prize money at events such as the DIR-V Grand Challenge. Each winning product built on these processors becomes a small proof point that Indian teams can design and deploy usable hardware on domestically developed silicon, rather than only assembling around imported chips.
Taken together, the concluding session's announcements, layered on top of 41 MoUs and initiatives unveiled during the first two days, point to an event that MeitY is positioning as a bridge between policy intent and on-ground execution. With the EY-ISEA report setting a 2035 horizon for India's semiconductor ambitions, the next test will be whether winning startups such as Meevisai and Digiscope, and the skilling partnerships announced alongside them, can scale from hackathon prototypes and MoUs into deployable products and a trained workforce over the coming years.

articles.title: Delonghi Rivelia Start : une version plus abordable pour démocratiser cette excellente machine à café à grains
articles.text:
Delonghi Rivelia Start : une version plus abordable pour démocratiser cette excellente machine à café à grains
Delonghi décline sa machine à café automatique avec broyeur dans une nouvelle version moins onéreuse. Pour contenir son prix, l’appareil fait l’impasse sur certaines fonctionnalités tout en conservant les fondamentaux de la gamme.
Delonghi enrichit sa gamme Rivelia. La marque italienne lance la Rivelia Start, une nouvelle machine à café automatique avec broyeur dérivée de la Rivelia Latte.
La Start en reprend l'esthétique et les principales caractéristiques, mais fait l'impasse sur certains éléments présents chez son aînée. Le principal sacrifice est visible dès que l’on regarde la façade : pour accéder aux principaux modes et réglages, l’écran tactile couleur de 3,5 pouces proposé par la version Latte fait désormais place à des commandes sensitives.
Delonghi Rivelia Start
En outre, la Start ne permet plus de créer plusieurs profils d'utilisateurs ni d’enregistrer des routines pour adapter les recettes aux habitudes de chacun au fil de la journée. Son choix de boissons se limite à 10 spécialités (Cappuccino, Flat White, Latte Macchiato, Expresso…) contre 16 pour la Rivelia Latte.
Un prix plus accessible, mais une expérience simplifiée
Ce positionnement permet à Delonghi de commercialiser son appareil au prix indicatif de 649,99 euros contre 799 euros pour la version Latte. Une différence de 149 euros qui peut se justifier pour les utilisateurs qui n’ont pas besoin de plusieurs profils ou de routines personnalisées.
En revanche, pour une machine proposée à près de 650 euros, l’absence d’écran tactile et la réduction du nombre de boissons disponibles sont des concessions à prendre en compte avant l’achat. La Rivelia Start conserve néanmoins plusieurs éléments importants de la gamme.
Le Bean Switch System est de retour, avec ses deux bacs à grains interchangeables de 250 g fournis à l’achat. Un système pratique pour alterner entre deux cafés, par exemple un mélange classique le matin et un café décaféiné en soirée, sans avoir à vider le bac à grains.
La Rivelia Start devra trouver sa place face à la Latte
La Start introduit également une nouveauté : la préparation de Cold Brew en moins de 5 minutes, souligne Delonghi. La Rivelia Latte n'embarquait pas cette fonction.
La Rivelia Start conserve aussi le système LatteCrema Hot qui prépare automatiquement une mousse de lait chaude pour les cappuccinos, Flat White et autres Latte Macchiato. Après chaque utilisation, la machine lance automatiquement un cycle de rinçage pour éliminer les résidus et faciliter son entretien.
Avec la Rivelia Start, Delonghi ouvre une nouvelle porte d’entrée vers sa famille de machines automatiques. Reste à voir comment la Rivelia Start se positionnera face à la Rivelia Latte. On l'a dit, à 649,99 euros, elle coûte 149 euros de moins que sa grande soeur. Cependant, l’écart pourrait rapidement se réduire si la version Latte est régulièrement proposée en promotion. Dans ce cas, la Start perdrait une partie de son intérêt puisqu’il serait possible d’obtenir une machine plus complète pour quelques dizaines d’euros supplémentaires.

articles.title: Binance : Christina Lagarde aurait pesé pour bloquer l'obtention de la licence MiCA
articles.text:
La patronne de la BCE a encore eu de l'impact dans le secteur des cryptomonnaies. Cette fois, elle aurait pesé sur le dossier Binance.
C'est une nouvelle qui n'a pas été très bonne pour de nombreux crypto bros français. Binance, la plus grande plateforme de cryptomonnaies au monde, n'a pas obtenu sa licence MiCA au début de l'été, ce qui dans la pratique l'empêche d'opérer au niveau du Vieux Continent. Un dossier qui aurait été bloqué par personne d'autres que la patronne de la BCE, Christine Lagarde.
Christine Lagarde aurait demandé au premier ministre grec de ne pas octroyer la licence MiCA
On connaît les critiques de Christine Lagarde contre les cryptomonnaies. On apprend aujourd'hui, grâce à une information du Wall Street Journal, qu'elle a aussi été d'une influence prépondérante pour empêcher l'obtention de la licence MiCA pour Binance.
En effet, le média américain narre une histoire en trois temps. D'abord, la plateforme Binance avait presque atteint son but avec les autorités grecques, et avait même produit un communiqué laissant entendre que la licence MiCA était sur le point d'être autorisée. Mais quelques jours plus tard, Christine Lagarde est intervenue directement auprès du premier ministre Kyriákos Mitsotákis, pour lui demander de ne pas approuver cette demande.
La volonté de mieux protéger l'euro numérique
Or, si l'organe de régulation grec, le Hellenic Capital Market Commission (HCMC), est indépendant, il avait aussi précisé qu'il ne donnerait pas de licence sans l'approbation du premier ministre. Après des efforts infrucuteux de dernières minutes de la part de Binance, la plateforme a finalement décidé de retirer sa demande.
Selon le même média, Christine Lagarde voulait laisser sur le côté la plateforme crypto ayant plaidé coupable aux États-Unis pour des faits de blanchiment d'argent. Elle aurait aussi voulu protéger le développement du futur euro numérique, voyant dans Binance une plateforme qui pourrait renforcer les rivaux que sont les stablecoins en dollar.

articles.title: Pagas una cerveza y tienes IA ilimitada: así funciona el curioso bar de la inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
Pagar una cerveza y recibir acceso a inteligencia artificial ilimitada mientras permaneces en el establecimiento. Esa es la idea detrás de los llamados bares de IA, un concepto que empieza a aparecer en distintos mercados y que plantea una nueva forma de acceder a herramientas de inteligencia artificial.
La propuesta es sencilla: el cliente consume una bebida y, como parte del servicio, puede utilizar la infraestructura de IA disponible en el local. En lugar de pagar por una suscripción o contratar capacidad de procesamiento en la nube, tiene acceso a los recursos del establecimiento durante su estancia.
PUBLICIDAD
El concepto ya se está dando en países como Estados Unidos, Inglaterra, Japón, Alemania y China, aunque las características de cada espacio pueden variar. El punto en común es convertir la inteligencia artificial en un servicio que se ofrece dentro de un establecimiento físico.
Una cafetería que también ofrece capacidad de IA
La diferencia con una cafetería convencional no está solamente en tener Wi-Fi. Estos espacios incorporan equipos capaces de ejecutar modelos de inteligencia artificial y permiten que los clientes los utilicen desde sus propios dispositivos.
Una persona puede llegar con su ordenador, conectarse a la infraestructura del local y utilizar los recursos disponibles para diferentes tareas. Programación, generación de contenido, análisis de información o experimentación con modelos de IA son algunos de los usos posibles.
PUBLICIDAD
El acceso puede gestionarse mediante una red local, un código QR u otros sistemas habilitados por el establecimiento. El consumo de recursos se mide mediante tokens, aunque en determinados casos el usuario puede recibir una cantidad ilimitada mientras permanezca en el local.
El bar como nuevo espacio de trabajo
La propuesta también cambia la función tradicional de estos establecimientos. Un bar de IA puede convertirse en un punto de encuentro para desarrolladores, estudiantes, investigadores y emprendedores que necesitan utilizar herramientas de inteligencia artificial mientras trabajan.
La bebida deja de ser el único producto que se ofrece. El establecimiento también pone a disposición del cliente una infraestructura tecnológica que normalmente tendría que contratar por separado.
PUBLICIDAD
La idea se acerca así al funcionamiento de los espacios de coworking, pero con un componente adicional: en lugar de limitarse a proporcionar mesas, conexión a internet y un ambiente de trabajo, el local ofrece acceso a capacidad de procesamiento para inteligencia artificial.
Una tendencia que comienza a extenderse
La aparición de este modelo en diferentes países apunta a una búsqueda de nuevas formas de acercar la inteligencia artificial al público.
No significa que todos funcionen de la misma manera ni que exista un modelo único de bar de IA. Algunos pueden centrarse en determinadas herramientas, mientras que otros ofrecen acceso a infraestructura de computación para que los clientes trabajen con sus propios proyectos.
PUBLICIDAD
La idea central, sin embargo, es la misma: llevar la IA fuera de la pantalla y convertir su capacidad de procesamiento en un servicio disponible en un espacio físico.
El desafío está en los costes
El modelo también enfrenta un problema evidente. Mantener equipos capaces de ejecutar modelos de IA implica gastos importantes en hardware, electricidad, refrigeración y mantenimiento.
Pese a ello, este concepto muestra cómo la inteligencia artificial puede empezar a integrarse en lugares cotidianos. Del mismo modo que una cafetería ofrece actualmente Wi-Fi como parte de su servicio, estos establecimientos buscan que el acceso a la capacidad de IA sea otro elemento de la experiencia.
PUBLICIDAD
El resultado es un nuevo tipo de espacio híbrido: un lugar para tomar algo, trabajar y, al mismo tiempo, utilizar infraestructura de inteligencia artificial sin necesidad de instalarla o contratarla directamente.

articles.title: Solidigm Reportedly Plans Its First NAND Fab in the United States
articles.text:
Sunday, September 20th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Solidigm Reportedly Plans Its First NAND Fab in the United States
SK hynix subsidiary Solidigm is reportedly planning to open its first NAND Flash manufacturing facility in the United States. To address global supply chain challenges, SK hynix is exploring ways to expand its production capabilities worldwide and create a more resilient operation against geopolitical events. Currently, Solidigm operates in the United States with its headquarters and R&D center, while all its manufacturing is based outside the country. When SK hynix acquired Intel's NAND Flash manufacturing business in 2021 and established the Solidigm brand, the company continued manufacturing in China without expanding overseas.
At present, Solidigm operates Fab 1 in Dalian, China, and has accelerated the construction of Fab 2 nearby. This expansion aims to increase production by 50% by 2027 to meet the rising demand for NAND Flash. Solidigm owns and operates this facility, marking a resumption of expansion in mainland China after a four-year project freeze.Currently, Solidigm produces about 100,000 wafers per month of NAND Flash, so a 50% increase by 2027 would boost production to approximately 150,000 wafers per month. Solidigm will also begin producing its floating gate 3D QLC NAND Flash, which will feature over 200 active storage layers per chip. This advancement will enable multi-terabyte SSDs for enterprise use, which is currently the primary market for these solutions. While QLC NAND Flash is slower than the typical TLC variant and has less endurance, AI workloads are demanding more capacity at higher densities.

articles.title: North Korea used job interviews to deploy malware on 30,000 devices during coding tests — WaterPlum group loots $10.7 million in crypto and plants persistent RATs
articles.text:
North Korea used job interviews to deploy malware on 30,000 devices during coding tests — WaterPlum group loots $10.7 million in crypto and plants persistent RATs
If it's too good to be true, it probably is.
Security agencies in Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany warned that the North Korean “WaterPlum” cyber actor group has been installing malware on applicants to fake job postings and stealing their credentials and cryptocurrency holdings. The advisory [PDF] says more than 30,000 devices across 100 countries have already been infected and more than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets have been compromised, leading to losses of $10.71 million.
It’s believed the stolen cryptocurrency was funneled to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) government, which also uses fake IT personnel working at legitimate companies to net $500 million annually. The operation also steals credentials and personal data, which it later uses to apply for openings at Western companies. Amazon has seen an example of this in late 2025, with over 1,800 suspected North Korean applications blocked by the company since April 2024.
The attacks occur when fake recruiters ask legitimate applicants to complete coding assignments and other tests to evaluate their skills. However, these often have hidden malware that gives the attackers access to the victim’s computer. These persistent remote access trojans (RATs) allow the WaterPlum group to access an infected system even months after the interview. Since the compromised computer is likely the same device that the targeted applicant will use once they get a legitimate job at another company, it could also be used by the North Koreans as a springboard to attack the systems of and steal credentials from their future clients.
International agencies say these fake recruiters often target software developers and IT professionals with attractive openings, using the names of legitimate AI, cryptocurrency, and NFT companies and posting openings on online job platforms, social media, gig work platforms, and freelance marketplaces. These fake IT workers and similar schemes are used by the hermit kingdom to generate revenue, especially since it has been largely excluded from the wider international economy due to sanctions.
Many companies are aware of this and are taking steps to protect themselves against similar tactics, but it’s probably harder for individual users who are simply looking for opportunities online to do so. Potential applicants can protect themselves by applying only directly with the company and on legitimate platforms, and if they’re unsure about an opening, they should contact the company directly to confirm its legitimacy. If they decide to go to an interview, it would also be wise to set up an isolated virtual machine just for that purpose, giving them an additional layer of protection against potential attacks.

Tonight's UFC 331 headline bout is a classic case of revenge or repeat as Joshua Van puts the UFC flyweight title he won against Alexandre Pantoja on the line at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The Fearless won the belt in controversial fashion in December 2025 and the Cannibal is determined to right the wrong he has felt ever since.

articles.title: En Japón están hartos de los turistas que se pierden en el monte Fuji. Así que empezará a cobrarles por los rescates
articles.text:
Si te pierdes en el Fuji por recorrer sus senderos de forma imprudente e ignorando los consejos de las autoridades locales, paga. Esa es la filosofía que quiere aplicar la prefectura de Yamanashi, en Chūbu, una de las administraciones que supervisa las rutas de escalada. Harto de los accidentes protagonizados por excursionistas y ante el aumento del turismo, el Gobierno regional ha decidido cobrar por los rescates que exijan movilizar un helicóptero en temporada baja.
No se sabe aún a cuánto ascenderá la tarifa, pero en la vecina prefectura de Saitama ya se aplica una medida similar y su tarifa ronda los 8.000 yenes (45 euros) por cada cinco minutos de vuelo. En la práctica, eso hizo que la factura media de cada operación de rescate superase el año pasado los 640 euros.
El dato: 300.000 excursionistas. Japón tiene algunos iconos reconocidos a nivel mundial, como las puertas Torii, el festival de Sakura, el cruce de Shibuya o el barrio de las geishas de Kioto (por citar solo un puñadod e ejemplos), pero ninguno es equiparable al Fuji, seguramente su signo más emblemático.
Eso explica que cada verano recorran sus cuatro senderos principales entre 200.000 y 300.000 personas, según datos de la Oficina Nacional de Turismo (JNTO). Y dado que el país no para de recibir visitantes extranjeros y aspira a llegar a los 60 millones en 2030, es probable que esa cifra siga creciendo.
Goteo de rescates. El problema es que no todos los excursionistas (locales y extranjeros) afrontan la escalada al Fuji igual. Los hay que planifican de forma detallada su expedición, entrenan y siguen los consejos de las autoridades locales, y luego hay también senderistas imprudentes que no hacen nada de eso. Según el diario Japan Times, entre 2018 y 2025 se registraron una veintena de accidentes de escalada (con cuatro fallecidos) solo en la vertiente de Yamanashi.
No es el único dato que demuestra el desafío que encara Yamanashi. Desde 2020 las autoridades locales han tenido que movilizar su helicóptero de rescates en tres ocasiones distintas en meses que, en teoría, se consideran de temporada baja.
Cuestión de calendario. Ese último matiz (el de la temporada) es importante porque el Fuji no es igual de transitable durante todo el año: la temporada oficial para las escaladas suele ir de finales de junio a principios de septiembre. Fuera de esos meses la escalada no es ilegal, pero las estaciones de mayor altitud de las cuatro rutas principales están cerradas y muchos refugios fuera de servicio.
Eso sin contar con que las condiciones meteorológicas en el Fuji son mucho peores, lo que lleva al Gobierno a rogar "encarecidamente" que la gente no suba. No solo por su propia seguridad. También por la de los rescatistas. "Quiero que la gente piense en quienes tienen que ir a salvarlos. Es de sentido común. Por favor, piensen en quienes deben realizar rescates arriesgando sus propias vidas y en la preocupación de sus familias", insiste el gobernador, Kotaro Nagasak.
Si metes la pata, pagas. La prefectura de Yamanashi, que supervisa las rutas de escalada junto a la vecina Shizuoka, se ha cansado del goteo de senderistas que intentan ascender el Fuji en los peores meses del año y ha dicho 'basta'. El lunes anunció que empezará a cobrar a quienes se quedan atrapados en la montaña y necesitan un helicóptero. El objetivo: disuadir a los visitantes imprudentes y, si eso no funciona, que al menos el coste de su rescate no les salga gratis.
El planteamiento es en realidad muy sencillo: si quieres subir al Fuji en temporada baja, de septiembre a junio, y planteas ir más allá de la sexta estación del sendero Yoshiba, tendrás que rellenar un formulario. En él deberás concretar tu plan de ascenso y el equipo que emplearás. Si el Gobierno regional considera que no está bien podrá recomendarte algunos cambios. Ese documento es clave porque puede marcar la diferencia entre pagar o no cientos de euros.
¿Y eso, por qué? Porque si al final te quedas atrapado en la montaña y necesitas que la prefectura movilice su helicóptero, ese formulario resultará decisivo, según avanza la prensa local. Los senderistas que no hayan presentado su plan de ascenso o lo hayan ignorado, desviándose de la ruta o desoyendo las recomendaciones, se arriesgarán a pagar la factura del rescate. Si los expertos consideran que han actuado de forma temeraria correrán el mismo riesgo.
El plan del gobierno de Yamanashi aún debe perfilarse, pero Asashi desliza que aquellos montañistas responsables que cumplen todas las recomendaciones y sencillamente tienen mala suerte durante su ascenso al Fuji podrían verse exentos de la factura del rescate o, al menos, abonarían tarifas reducidas.
8.000 yenes por cinco minutos. Quedan todavía algunas incógnitas por resolver, como el coste que tendrán las operaciones de rescate de Yamanashi. En cualquier caso, no parten de cero. En la vecina prefectura de Saitama ya aplican una medida similar desde 2018 y allí se cobra 8.000 yenes (45 euros) por cada cinco minutos de vuelo del helicóptero, lo que explica que la factura media de los cinco rescates realizados en 2025 ascendiera a 115.000 yenes, unos 640 euros.
En teoría, la medida empezará a aplicarse en septiembre de 2027.
Lo cierto es que el debate sobre cómo afrontar los rescates de turistas imprudentes en el Fuji lleva tiempo sobre la mesa de las autoridades japonesas. No solo eso. La turistificación de la montaña también ha llevado al Gobierno a plantearse el cobro de una tarifa por ascender al Fuji, una forma re recaudar fondos para, entre otras cosas, eliminar la basura que se acumula la zona.

articles.title: Connections and conversations: How effective curation creates impact for art exhibitions
articles.text:
Connections and conversations: How effective curation creates impact for art exhibitions
In this photo essay, we showcase artistic highlights from the ‘One | Many’ exhibition at the India Habitat Centre.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,015 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
The India Habitat Centre (IHC) recently hosted the art exhibition titled ‘One | Many’ (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at this popular cultural hub in New Delhi here). Curated by artist Pabitra Pal, it featured the works of 12 artists.
Such exhibitions illustrate how an effective curator connects artworks, artists, ideas, and audiences (see also Part I of our photo essay on this showcase). Tactful and strategic selection, interpretation and presentation of artworks can create a meaningful exhibition experience.
A curator connects artworks to history, culture, social issues, artistic movements, and the artist's practice. This helps audiences discover deeper interpretations of diverse art works.
Furthermore, thoughtful placement, sequencing, lighting, labels, and spatial design influence how visitors move through the exhibition and engage with the displayed works. Such placements encourage dialogue and create opportunities for reflection and learning.
Over the years, Pabitra Pal and his artistic community have organised and participated in many exhibitions. “Our latest exhibition, ‘One | Many’, became our 28th group exhibition,” Pal tells YourStory, with pride.
When he moved from Kolkata to New Delhi in 2010, he joined the artistic collective called The Mirror Group. It was established in 2002 by Dev Dutta, Susnato Chatterjee, and other artists.
The present group, some of whose artworks are showcased here, includes Dev Dutta, Debangsu Biswas, Susnato Chatterjee, Titas Das, and Soumen Basu. “We have known each other for more than 25 years, and our friendship has grown alongside our artistic practices,” Pal affirms.
“We regularly invite other artists to join us, share ideas, and celebrate the continuing journey. For us, the group is a space for friendship, discussion, exchange, and artistic growth,” he adds.
Curators thus build artistic and cultural value by bringing to the fore new artists and challenging established conventions. But all this is easier said than done.
Exhibition curators can face challenges in balancing artistic quality, diversity, theme, and the overall story without overcrowding the exhibition. Managing limited funds, gallery dimensions, transportation, insurance, installation, and deadlines are other tasks to manage.
From an audience point of view, the exhibition should be accessible to different levels of knowledge – while also preserving artistic depth and complexity. Curators need to be conscious of avoiding tokenism while addressing cultural sensitivities.
Curators therefore need to begin by defining the central question or theme, and mapping out what the exhibition wants visitors to think, feel or discover. In addition to quality and relevance of the individual artworks, relationships between the exhibits also need to enabled.
The exhibition space should support the art rather than compete or interfere with it. Varied interpretive materials will be needed, which can involve testing and experimentation with audiences from different backgrounds.
Observing visitor responses and reflecting on their feedback helps reveal insights for future exhibitions. A great exhibition is thus more than a collection of artworks – it is a carefully constructed conversation between art, artist, space, and audience.
Curator Pal’s own artistic journey began at the age of 12. “I grew up near Kolkata, West Bengal, where village and city life came together. This early experience created a strong connection between myself, nature and everyday life,” he recalls.
He later moved to Santiniketan to study at Kala Bhavana, Visva Bharati University. “Being surrounded by artists, teachers and scholars gave me the opportunity to exchange ideas, observe different artistic practices, and develop my own way of seeing,” he explains.
“My practice has developed through drawing, printmaking, painting, and three-dimensional work. I regularly experiment with different materials and techniques, but I view the medium as mainly a tool to express an idea,” Pal affirms.
His artworks connect memory, nature, everyday experience, and dreams. “Over the years, travelling and living in different places in India has also influenced my artistic thinking. My interactions and discussions with other artists have helped me continue my research and develop my practice,” he adds.
Pal has participated in more than 35 exhibitions in India and overseas, and won a string of awards. “I work as an art educator and teach visual arts through the IB curriculum. Teaching, research, observation, and making art continue to influence one another in my journey,” he explains.
“For me, making art is an ongoing process of looking, experimenting, questioning, and discovering. Each artwork develops through this process, where the material, image, memory, and idea gradually come together,” Pal says.
He also offers tips for aspiring artists “Everyone is creative — you just have to nurture it. Draw, doodle, paint, sculpt, do anything that helps you grow,” he suggests.
“Don't worry about being perfect; just keep creating, a little every day. When you travel, visit the museums of the city — they teach you about culture, heritage and the soul of a place,” he adds.
There is beauty all around. “When you see something beautiful in nature, don't just click a photo. Pause. Look with your own eyes. Make a small sketch instead. A photo is a copy, but a sketch holds your feeling, your time, your memory — something you will treasure forever,” he describes.
“Art is not about talent alone. It is about practice, patience and love for what you do," he says.
"So keep your hands busy and your heart open. The world needs your creativity,” Pal signs off.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at IHC.)

articles.title: Greensand, l'immense site de stockage de CO2 mis en service au Danemark
articles.text:
Enterrer le CO2, c'est une des options sur la table depuis de nombreuses années pour réduire les émissions de ce gaz à effet de serre, à l'origine du dérèglement climatique. Mais cette technologie coûte cher, et est encore assez peu appliquée. En Europe, on voit finalement un premier site d'ampleur commencer à fonctionner pour capturer le dioxyde de carbone.
Greensand, le premier site majeur de stockage de CO2 européen, voit le jour
C'est une première qui a eu lieu ce vendredi 18 septembre du côté du Danemark. Le projet d'enfouissement de CO2 Greensand vient d'y être inauguré, avec l'installation qui a commencé à enterrer le gaz à effet de serre sous une ancienne plateforme pétrolière de la mer de Nord.
Un projet piloté par le géant de la chimie et des hydrocarbures Ineos, qui « prouve que le stockage du carbone est une réalité concrète », selon les mots du commissaire européen à l'énergie, Dan Jorgensen. La capture de CO2 est notamment intéressante pour les secteurs d'activité difficiles à décarboner, à l'image de l'indusrie cimentière.
Un équipement qui pourra rapidement stocker de 4 à 8 millions de tonnes de CO2 par an
« Aujourd'hui, Greensand met en service le premier site de stockage de CO2 à grande échelle de l'UE […]. Il offre une base sur laquelle les futurs projets de captage du carbone à travers l'Europe peuvent désormais s’appuyer » a de son côté déclaré dans un communiqué le directeur général d'Ineos, David Bucknall.
Le site Greensand va, dans un premier temps, être en capacité de stocker 400 000 tonnes de CO2 par an - une capacité qui montera ensuite d'ici 2030 à 4 à 8 millions de tonnes de CO2 stockés annuellement. Ce dioxyde de carbone proviendra en majorité des centrales de biométhane du royaume danois.

On ne pourra diminuer sa production qu’à la marge. Des pays émergents immenses, comme le Brésil, sont à des années lumière de se lancer dans cette démarche. Comme l’Inde. On ne peut pas penser cette problématique en réfléchissant comme si le monde était comme la France, désindustrialisé et à la traine en matière de croissance. Nous, on peut se permettre de mettre quelques éloliennes pour remplir des objectifs fixés par Bruxelles, tout en étant certain que ça ne règlera pas le problème. Les pays émergents n’ont pas ce luxe et ils sont très nombreux. Ils ont une population à sortir de la misère. Ils ne pourront pas le faire sans émettre des quantités phénoménales de CO2. Quel est l’impact réel sur l’environnement ?
La Chine produit 12,5 milliards de tonnes de CO2 par an, et ses émissions continuent de progresser. À ce rythme, même en fonctionnant à pleine capacité pendant 1 500 ans, ce site ne parviendraient pas à extraire de l’atmosphère ce que la Chine rejette en une seule année. Il faudrait des milliers de site comme ça. J’ai raté quelque chose?

Bien d’accord. Cela ressemble à du greenwashing (comme souvent).
frigolu
Oui, on préfère dépenser des milliards pour tenter de compenser (à peine) la destruction massive que nous occasionnons, plutôt que de changer radicalement notre mode de vie (ola, surtout pas, parlez pas de malheur, la nature, toussa, quelle horreur, vive les iPhone et mon petit cocon virtuel !). Les penseurs qui arguent que le concept « d’intelligence » que l’homo sapiens s’est inventé pour se mettre en avant ne serait en réalité qu’une tare de l’évolution, une capacité de destruction et d’auto-destruction (qui le mènera à sa propre extinction), semblent particulièrement lucides. (Re)lisez Günther Anders, Zapffe, E.O Wilson. Et regardez ce que nous faisons de la Terre, du vivant, comment nous traitons tout comme de la m…, comme si tout nous était dû, tout ça pour des concepts, de l’argent, des possessions matérielles toutes plus inutiles les unes que les autres. Nous nous comportons « comme un virus » d’après le film Matrix. Nous ne sommes que des barbares primitifs qui se donnent des airs d’espèce évoluée, à l’instar du Gremlin intello dans Gremlins II. Le pire, c’est dès que les gens forment des groupes. (Re)lisez aussi Gustave Le Bon, ou Pierre Kropotkine (sur l’entraide plutôt que la compétition).
Tholar
Vous me faites marrer, tous, avec vos petits complexes d’occidentaux lovés dans le confort, leur logement aux normes et leur carte Vitale dans le portefeuille. Vous croyez que le reste du monde ne veut pas le même confort que vous ? Il a fallu émettre des milliards de milliards de tonnes de CO2 pour atteindre ce confort ! Et maintenant que vous l’avez, vous voudriez que le reste du monde n’ait pas la même chose que vous ? Il va falloir trouver une autre solution que de diminuer les émissions de CO2, parce qu’elles ne vont pas diminuer.
Kurton
Tu as grandement raison sauf sur un point. Lorsque les nations les plus avancées industriellement ont progressé, elles ont fait avec les moyens qu’elles avaient. Maintenant, les nations émergentes, qui ont totalement le droit de vouloir se mettre à niveau, peuvent aussi profiter des acquis des sociétés plus avancées. C’est un des objectifs majeursdu G7 entre autres.
Maintenant, les émissions de CO2 vont baisser dans les 2 décennies (je pense) qui viennent pour 2 raisons possibles : l’humanité s’adapte et réduit grandement sa production de CO2 ou une partie de l’humanité meurt par manque d’adaptation. Ce n’est pas tant que la température sera insupportable mais plutôt que la production de nourriture et l’eau va devenir extrêmement compliquée, vu que la fréquence des périodes de canicules va augmenter.
Bon, je dramatise peut être mais quand on pense réchauffement climatique, on pense température à un instant T, mais on projette beaucoup moins la fréquence ses effets destructeurs sur la production de nourriture et les stockes d’eau.

Est-ce qu’il compensera les turbines à gaz géantes d’Amazon au Texas ?
Andreia
Une position louable mais dont on a vu avec l’Iran que la condition sine qua non de l’accès aux technologies de pointe reste la soumission intégrale aux nations qui les possèdent.

articles.title: Una copia digital del cerebro de una mosca ya juega Doom y toma decisiones sobre criptomonedas
articles.text:
Científicos lograron reconstruir en formato digital el cerebro y el sistema nervioso central completo de una mosca de la fruta adulta y, poco después, desarrolladores comenzaron a utilizar este modelo para realizar experimentos que van desde jugar al clásico videojuego Doom hasta tomar decisiones sobre operaciones con criptomonedas.
El mapa digital, denominado MaleCNS v1.0, reúne más de 166.000 neuronas, alrededor de 125 millones de conexiones entre ellas y cerca de 11.700 tipos de células. El trabajo fue realizado por investigadores de Google Research, el HHMI Janelia Research Campus, Harvard y Princeton, y representa un avance importante para estudiar cómo una red neuronal biológica procesa información.
PUBLICIDAD
La reconstrucción no se limita al cerebro. También incluye el cordón nervioso de la mosca, una estructura comparable en algunos aspectos con la médula espinal humana. Esto permite analizar cómo la información puede recorrer el sistema nervioso desde la percepción de estímulos hasta la generación de respuestas motoras.
Un cerebro digital que aprendió a jugar Doom
Tras la publicación de MaleCNS v1.0, desarrolladores comenzaron a utilizar el conectoma en diferentes simulaciones. Una de las más llamativas fue desarrollada por el ingeniero Alex Wormuth, quien conectó el modelo digital con Doom, el conocido videojuego de disparos.
En la simulación, cada imagen del videojuego se transforma en señales que estimulan las neuronas sensoriales del cerebro virtual. El sistema procesa miles de señales de brillo y color que activan millones de conexiones neuronales para generar decisiones de control dentro del juego.
PUBLICIDAD
El experimento también incorpora un mecanismo similar al aprendizaje por refuerzo. Cuando el personaje recibe un daño que no provoca su muerte, determinadas células dopaminérgicas actúan como una señal de recompensa o refuerzo dentro de la simulación.
Otros desarrolladores han utilizado el mismo modelo en experimentos relacionados con videojuegos como Super Mario 64 y Beat Saber.
También lo utilizaron para operar con criptomonedas
El conectoma digital también salió del terreno de los videojuegos. Wormuth creó el proyecto Stonkfly, que utiliza el cerebro simulado de la mosca para analizar gráficos financieros y tomar decisiones en operaciones con criptomonedas.
La simulación incorpora señales que funcionan como recompensas y castigos. Cuando la cartera virtual obtiene ganancias, se activa una señal asociada a 15 células neuronales. Las pérdidas, en cambio, activan dos células relacionadas con respuestas aversivas.
PUBLICIDAD
El modelo también ha sido utilizado en otros experimentos realizados por desarrolladores, como la clasificación de correos electrónicos, la resolución de salas de escape y la creación de tipografías.
En una prueba de clasificación de mensajes, el cerebro digital alcanzó alrededor del 80 % de la precisión obtenida por una pequeña red neuronal artificial convencional. El resultado muestra que una red biológica reconstruida puede utilizarse para procesar determinados patrones, aunque eso no significa que pueda competir con los sistemas de IA diseñados específicamente para esas tareas.
Cómo reconstruyeron el cerebro de la mosca
Para crear MaleCNS v1.0, los investigadores tuvieron que dividir el sistema nervioso de la mosca en miles de secciones extremadamente delgadas. Cada una fue fotografiada mediante microscopía electrónica, generando millones de imágenes.
PUBLICIDAD
Posteriormente, herramientas de inteligencia artificial permitieron alinear y ensamblar esas imágenes para reconstruir una representación tridimensional del sistema nervioso con precisión celular.
El resultado funciona como un enorme mapa de conexiones conocido como conectoma. Este permite conocer qué neuronas están conectadas entre sí y estudiar la estructura de la red, pero no equivale a tener un cerebro biológico vivo funcionando dentro de un ordenador.
El cerebro digital tiene importantes límites
Los experimentos no significan que los científicos hayan creado una mosca digital consciente. MaleCNS v1.0 es fundamentalmente un mapa estático de conexiones y necesita simulaciones adicionales para producir comportamientos.
Además, el sistema fue diseñado por la evolución para las necesidades de una mosca, por lo que sus capacidades disminuyen cuando se le asignan tareas alejadas de las funciones para las que evolucionó.
PUBLICIDAD
Los investigadores y desarrolladores también han encontrado que ejecutar este modelo puede ser más lento y menos preciso que utilizar redes neuronales artificiales creadas específicamente para cada objetivo.
Por ahora, el principal valor del proyecto está en permitir estudiar cómo una red neuronal biológica completa puede transformar estímulos en respuestas. Los experimentos con videojuegos y criptomonedas son una demostración llamativa de esa posibilidad, pero todavía están lejos de demostrar que una simulación de un cerebro biológico pueda reproducir la experiencia subjetiva de un animal.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: La "línea de visión" más larga de todo el planeta: una fotografía real de Turquía vista a 500 kilómetros desde el Cáucaso
articles.text:
El Shkhara está en el Cáucaso, tiene 5.193 metros de altura, es la montaña más alta de Georgia y hace muga con Rusia. El Karagöl es una cadena montañosa turca situada en el noreste de Turquía, en la provincia de Giresun, en la región del mar Negro, con su cima principal a 3.107 metros. Entre un pico y otro hay casi 500 kilómetros de distancia, una auténtica barbaridad imposible de divisar con el ojo humano. Pero no con una cámara y bajo ciertas condiciones.
Una línea de visión de récord. Pues bien, el 15 de diciembre de 2024, el fotógrafo eslovaco Richard Jezik logró capturar el Shkhara desde un subpico cercano al Karagöl y batió un récord: la línea de visión más larga de todo el planeta Tierra, certificado por Guinness World Records, con 493,07 kilómetros. Nunca antes el ojo humano había visto tan lejos... con ayuda de un teleobjetivo, claro. La foto es verdaderamente impresionante.
Hacer una fotografía así no es algo que pase por casualidad, porque te llevas tu cámara mientras haces senderismo: Jezik lleva documentando este tipo de observaciones desde 2018 y persiguiendo esta foto desde 2023. Porque para conseguir este documento gráfico necesitó sangre, sudor y lágrimas: ascender hasta la cima a pie porque la nieve impedía el acceso en coche, pasar la noche a -12°C con rachas de viento de hasta 20-25 m/s y esperar hasta el amanecer para apretar el disparador, explica el Guinness.
Cómo es posible. Esencialmente hay dos factores que explican que esta imagen sea físicamente posible:
- La geometría: cuanto más altos son los dos puntos, más lejos se puede ver antes de que la curvatura terrestre haga de las suyas. Ya hemos visto que el Shkhara ronda los 5.200 m, el subpico de Karagöl los 3.000 m. ¿La explicación? El alcance visual aumenta con la raíz cuadrada de la altitud.
- Una refracción atmosférica fuera de lo normal, como explica el físico Michael Vollmer: cuando hay aire frío pegado a la superficie con aire más cálido justo encima, la luz se curva siguiendo aproximadamente la curvatura de la Tierra, lo que permite ver más allá del horizonte para un avistamiento "extremo" como este.
La carrera por ver más lejos. Desde el Ezkaba de Ezkabarte, mi monte de referencia en Pamplona, los días despejados pueden llegar a verse los Pirineos a casi 100 kilómetros de distancia, pero eso no es nada comparado con lo que hacen estos fotógrafos especialistas en avistar largas distancias. Un par de ejemplos: en 2016, Marc Bret fotografió el macizo de los Écrins desde el Pic de Finestrelles en los Pirineos, a 443 kilómetros. En 2023, el chileno Roberto Antezana fotografió el Aconcagua desde el Cerro Champaquí, en Argentina, a una distancia de 483,5 kilómetros.
Hasta el infinito y más allá. Cada nuevo récord se ha establecido gracias a dos cosas: mejor tecnología fotográfica y comprender mejor el fenómeno de la refracción. Un par de trucos para llegar más lejos con tus fotografías de expertos en el fenómeno: mejor en invierno, de madrugada y sobre grandes masas de agua fría, justo lo que hizo Jezik.
Pero, ¿hasta dónde? El proyecto AllTheViews ha estimado cada visión posible de la Tierra y ha llegado a una conclusión: el punto con mayor alcance teórico del planeta sería una cresta sin nombre cerca de la frontera entre India y China, vista desde el Pik Dankova (Kirguistán), a algo más de 530 kilómetros.

articles.title: Sony FE 400mm F4.5 GM OSS : le super téléobjectif 400 mm le plus léger du marché
articles.text:
Sony FE 400mm F4.5 GM OSS : le super téléobjectif 400 mm le plus léger du marché
Le nouveau 400 mm de Sony sacrifie un peu d’ouverture pour offrir une qualité d’image G Master dans un objectif pesant moins d’un kilogramme. Idéal pour les photographes qui ont besoin d’être mobiles. Et qui ont le budget !
994 grammes : c'est le poids, sans collier de trépied, du nouveau FE 400mm F/4.5 GM OSS que Sony vient de dévoiler pour ses boîtiers Alpha. De quoi transformer la photographie animalière et sportive, jusqu'ici plutôt destinée aux porteurs de sacs à dos bien chargés, en une activité bien plus mobile.
Sony a déjà un 400 mm, mais c’est un monstre tant en termes de prix (12 000 € !) que de poids, puisqu’il pèse près de 3 kg (2895 g pour être précis). Le nouveau FE 400mm F/45 veut proposer une qualité d’image (bokeh f/2,8 en moins) approchante, avec son étiquette "G Master" (GM), mais dans un format plus compact et avec un poids quasiment divisé par trois.
Côté verre, le Japonais a conçu une formule optique complexe de 22 élément répartis en 16 groupes. Parmi elles, trois lentilles en verre Super ED (Extra-low Dispersion) qui limite les franges colorées et une lentille ED classique. À l’intérieur du fût de l’optique, le diaphragme circulaire à onze lames, hérité de la signature G Master, promet un bokeh très doux et progressif. Finalement, on apprécie que l'objectif soit compatible avec les téléconvertisseurs Sony x1,4 et x2, même s’il faudra alors accepter les pertes de luminosité (on passe respectivement à F/6,3 et F/9).
Orientée sport et nature, cette optique doit d’avoir du répondant. Pour faire la mise au point, elle intègre donc deux moteurs linéaires XD (extreme dynamic, la motorisation maison ultra rapide de Sony) épaulés par les algorithmes de reconnaissance IA des derniers boîtiers Alpha. Sony revendique une compatibilité totale avec la rafale à 120 images par seconde de l'Alpha 9 III, suivi en temps réel des sujets et compris.
Du point de vue physique, quatre boutons de verrouillage de mise au point, une bague de fonction et un limiteur de plage complètent l'ergonomie, le tout dans une conception tropicalisée – et la lentille frontale of course traitée au fluor.
Impossible d’écrire sur ce téléobjectif sans mentionner son inspiration, le NIKKOR Z 400mm F/4.5 VR S de Nikon, la référence sur le marché. Ce concurrent, Sony promet de le dépasser en termes de qualité d’image (les courbes MTF que Sony nous a montré sont effectivement meilleures), mais aussi en termes de poids (l’optique de Sony pèse 166g de moins) et de prix. Lancé à 2800 €, ce beau bébé est moins cher que les 3200 € actuels du Nikon (dont le prix officiel est de 3700 € !).
Le Sony FE 400 mm F/4.5 GM OSS sera commercialisé à partir de ce mois de septembre à 2800 €.

articles.title: Kash Patel says that AI use at the FBI has 'increased by 605%' since he became director — claims that every major tech player is 'embedded' in the agency
articles.text:
Kash Patel says that AI use at the FBI has 'increased by 605%' since he became director — claims that every major tech player is 'embedded' in the agency
A seemingly unsupported figure that nevertheless may be grounded in truth.
FBI Director Kash Patel just stated in an interview that he's responsible for a "605% increase" in the bureau's usage of AI. The problem is that while the pattern-recognition abilities of AI models make them an ideal candidate for use in law enforcement agencies, and It's a reasonable expectation that entities like the FBI would leverage the technology, it's hard to pin down what the 605% figure refers to.
The statement came up in an interview on Fox News, where Patel also said that AI, "when used lawfully, is a critical tool to triage data," remarking that the technology can be invaluable to assist in protecting children from school shootings. He credits AI as being instrumental in following up a lead to stop a shooting in North Carolina and "a half dozen other states" since his swearing-in.
It's hard to tell what Patel's seven-fold increase in AI could be referring to, as there appears to be little hard data about how much, and in what ways, AI is integrated into the bureau. Yet, there are a few leads that may help corroborate his claim.
The most recent details come from a February 2026 report about the DOJ's AI use case inventory in 2025, showing 50 of those attributed to the FBI, with nine marked as "high-impact." However, a more recent statement by the agency's Chief AI Officer Katie Noyes, in August, pinned approved use cases at 139, or close to three times the January amount.
Last year, the U.S. General Services Administration approved Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT as approved products, making them available to government agencies. Earlier this year in May, the Pentagon struck eight deals with AI companies as well. A few months ago, the FBI posted a procurement document asking for vendor proposals for $88 million's worth of AI servers, seemingly indicating that the agency is looking to expand its services.
But that may well be changing, as just a few days ago, on September 15, Patel claimed during a Senate hearing that he can directly contact major AI player's CEO, noting that "every single one of them has complied with our request and worked with us on law enforcement matters." Perhaps most importantly, he said that having access to vendors' models would make it easier to crack down on AI-assisted crime, seeing as criminal enterprises are rolling their own models, helped by distillation attacks.
The FBI now classifies AI-related crimes with its own descriptor, too, and highlights investment, romance, and employment as common areas of malfeasant activity in its latest Internet Crime Report. And in an op-ed published last May, Patel attributed a 30% increase in missing child locations and a 20% rise in child abuse arrests to the use of artificial intelligence tools, including facial recognition.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
He also wrote that the "FBI now uses new AI tools to generate call transcriptions, provide concise synopses and even help correlate contacts with other received complaints," highlighting that messages collected under a search warrant can take weeks to be processed by a cadre of analysts, something that AI can do with ease.
All told, these developments do seem to indicate that the bureau is indeed leveraging AI tools, even if Patel's "605%" figure needs a basis for comparison.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Steam Frame Gets First SteamOS Update With Substantially Faster Charging
articles.text:
Saturday, September 19th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Steam Frame Gets First SteamOS Update With Substantially Faster Charging
Valve has released SteamOS 0.3.0 for the Steam Frame, the headset's first system update since it launched on September 14. The changelog lists "substantially faster charging while unit is off / sleeping," which addresses a complaint that came up repeatedly in early reviews. The Verge tested the update and found the charging gains seem to go further than the changelog describes. Before the update, a depleted Steam Frame reportedly started charging at around 8 W and peaked at 27 W. Afterward, it starts at roughly 19 to 21 W and can reach 42 W while a game is running. Valve recommends a 45 W or faster USB-C charger, which is sold separately from the $1,059 headset.
The rest of the changelog also includes some important bits. The update improves controller tracking while haptics are active, improves stability and reliability under high load, and fixes a "garbled audio" microphone bug. The per-app Motion Smoothing "Force Always-On" setting was being ignored and should now work, and motion smoothing behavior in Half-Life: Alyx has been adjusted. For developers, Valve added Vulkan layer fixes and Mesa graphics performance work, and changed the Playable criteria to allow any resolution instead of requiring 1440p. Valve says the SteamOS update is available now for all users, but US and European purchase emails only began going out on September 18, so buyers may still have to wait a while.

articles.title: An undercover Google analyst infiltrated a notorious supply-chain hacking gang
articles.text:
Before two of its alleged members were arrested and charged in Australia last month, the hacker group known as TeamPCP carried out a hacking spree unlike any other in history. It tainted hundreds of open-source programs with its malware, stole developer accounts to perpetuate that software supply-chain hacking, and even released a Dune-themed self-spreading worm to automate the process, ultimately breaching more than a thousand companies.
Now Google’s threat intelligence group has revealed that during a key moment of TeamPCP’s rampage, the company’s own undercover researcher had infiltrated the group—allowing Google to monitor the hacking spree from the inside, warn breach targets, and even help disrupt the group’s attempts to exploit those victims.
In a talk at security firm SentinelOne’s LABScon research conference today, Google Threat Intelligence Group researcher Austin Larsen will present details on the company’s investigation—and infiltration—of TeamPCP amidst the group’s unprecedented, chaotic supply-chain hacking campaign. According to Larsen, Google eventually followed a trail of operational security mistakes allegedly made by one of the two Australians now accused of being leading members of the hacker group and passed on key identifying details to law enforcement. The company also received intelligence from ShinyHunters, another infamous cybercriminal group that TeamPCP partnered with, but which later turned on the supply-chain hackers. And perhaps most surprisingly, Larsen says that Google’s security subsidiary Mandiant had an undercover analyst—not himself—within the group’s inner circle from almost the beginning of TeamPCP’s time in the spotlight.
“One of our personas had been working for many months to build trust with one of the actors that was invited to join TeamPCP, and so was added to the group,” Larsen told WIRED in an interview ahead of his LABScon talk. “So essentially, almost day one, Mandiant was watching everything behind the scenes.”
The TeamPCP mole
Late last month, Ruben Ian Thomson and Louis Michael Gaebler, both Australians in their early 20s, were arrested by Australian police in a joint investigation with assistance from the FBI, charged with hacking crimes, and described by the Australian Federal Police (AFP)—in a press release that, due to Australian privacy laws, did not name them—as “principal participants” in TeamPCP. The hacker group, which seems to have first appeared online in late 2025, had made headlines with a brazen string of cascading supply-chain attacks: It repeatedly compromised open-source software to hide its malware, which then allowed it to hijack the credentials of software developers and plant its malicious code in yet another widely used tool, in a repeating cycle.
Starting this spring, for instance, TeamPCP compromised the open-source security scanner Trivy, the AI application programming interface tool LiteLLM, infrastructure of the web application security firm Checkmarx, the web app library TanStack, and the enterprise AI platform Mistral AI. Those repeated supply-chain attacks, with each enabling the group to cast its net again for more victims, ultimately allowed the hackers to breach open-source code repository GitHub, data contracting firm Mercor, and employee devices at OpenAI, the European Commission, and many others who have remained unnamed in public reporting. At times, the group deployed a worm known as Mini Shai-Hulud, named after the sandworms in Dune, to automate its hacking and scale up to even more victims. (The name also seemed to refer to an earlier Shai-Hulud worm that hackers designed to try a similar approach in September 2025, though it’s still not clear if TeamPCP or any of its alleged members were involved in that earlier intrusion campaign.)
Larsen now says that in March, just as TeamPCP was beginning its frenzied supply-chain hacking, Google’s own undercover analyst was invited to join the hackers’ inner circle. That inside source, whose name Larsen declined to reveal, was one of about 12 members of the group given access to a core chat that TeamPCP called CanisterWorm.
“You guys should understand that we pulled off the biggest supplychain [sic] maybe ever recorded in modern history,” one TeamPCP member wrote in the leaked chats.
Michael Fletcher, a former AFP analyst who now works in the threat research division of an Australian telecom firm, says he approached Larsen around that time about methods for monitoring the group’s members and activities. He says that Larsen responded by asking Fletcher to approach the hackers with caution because one of them was a “friendly,” Fletcher remembers. “I thought, damn, you all have been inside this early,” he says.
Google’s undercover analyst, Larsen says, gained access to a server where TeamPCP was storing its trove of credentials stolen from its many victims: the usernames, passwords, and access tokens it had obtained through its hacking and seemingly planned to use to extort target companies. So Google’s team decided to take action to warn victims and prevent TeamPCP’s ransom scheme. “My thought was: How can we, as quickly as possible, disrupt their campaign before more compromises can happen?” Larsen says. “Let’s go mess up what they’re doing. That was my goal.”
Rather than focus on alerting the owners of the stolen credentials at victim companies directly, which Larsen says would have taken too long given the sheer number of breached companies, Google first reached out to providers where those credentials could be used, like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, to have the credentials revoked and prevent the hackers from exploiting them. Larsen and his team sent out hundreds of notification emails to those providers and then to victims, many of which got immediate responses.
Around the same time, Larsen says, Google’s visibility into the TeamPCP internal chat also allowed it to learn that someone within the group’s core circle was, distinct from the group’s supply-chain hacking, using an AI tool to develop a zero-day exploit in a widely used piece of login software that would allow the hackers to bypass its two-factor authentication. Google’s team got a copy of the exploit code, tested it out, and found that, with a few tweaks, it worked—a rare instance of an in-the-wild AI-created hacking technique that took advantage of a previously unknown software vulnerability. Google warned the software’s developer, who was able to patch its security flaw. (The incident was described in a case study Google released in May, but without naming TeamPCP or detailing how Google learned about the exploit.)
More betrayals, sloppy opsec
Google’s analyst was not, it turns out, the only traitor in TeamPCP’s midst.
Even prior to Google’s disruption effort, Larsen says, the group struggled to profit from its enormous collection of stolen data, which, according to the AFP, included more than half a million users’ credentials. Larsen estimates that, despite that haul, it was pulling in only tens of thousands of dollars in extortion payments, not the millions similar groups have amassed. So in an attempt to better monetize its hacking, TeamPCP invited multiple other cybercriminal groups to partner with it, giving them access to the stolen credentials in exchange for a percentage of any extortion payments they were able to extract.
One of those cybercriminal partners was ShinyHunters, a years-old, highly prolific hacker group that has extorted millions of dollars from victims through data theft and ransomware, including in the breach of educational software platform Canvas that would later paralyze thousands of schools across the US. Around April, a few weeks after partnering with TeamPCP, ShinyHunters went rogue, Larsen says, carrying out its own extortions with TeamPCP’s credentials but without giving the supply-chain hackers their cut. ShinyHunters went so far as to share with Larsen, unsolicited, a full log of the group’s chat on TeamPCP’s server—not knowing that he already had access via Google’s mole.
ShinyHunters also taunted TeamPCP in messages on X, and its louder betrayal got the latter group’s attention. TeamPCP responded by narrowing its inner circle, moving its data to a new server, and exiling ShinyHunters and several other group members from its CanisterWorm chat, including Google’s undercover analyst.
“Just delete that and stop sharing shit with shinyhunters,” one of the TeamPCP leaders wrote.
Even without that inside source, though, Larsen says more traditional digital detective work allowed him to piece together the trail of breadcrumbs that would ultimately let him learn the identity of Thomson, one of the two men charged for allegedly playing “key” roles in TeamPCP. Larsen found in a leak of user data from the BreachForums hacker forum that one of the most active handles in the CanisterWorm chat had been registered with the Gmail address sheepstealing@gmail.com. Combing through other forum archives, he found a 2019 dispute between someone with the pseudonym sheepstealing and a seller of pirated Microsoft Office keys, in which the sheepstealing user demanded a refund at a PayPal account tied to the email ruben@thomsonfamily.net.au.
After TeamPCP moved its stolen credentials to a server hosted by a different provider, Larsen says, Google was able to learn about some contents of the new server—through what Larsen describes as a “trusted partner”—and also that it was being backed up to a Google Drive on that same sheepstealing@gmail.com account.
“When we saw that, I just thought: There’s no way. Why would he be sending all of this illicit, stolen material to a Google Drive that’s tied to himself?” Larsen says. “That’s when we gave the tip to the FBI.” Larsen says he got an interested response from an agent in a matter of minutes. (Larsen may not have been alone in identifying Thomson or other alleged TeamPCP hackers prior to their arrest. Journalist and cybersecurity sleuth Brian Krebs, for instance, published a story last month laying out his own set of clues that led to Thomson’s identity.
In a statement to WIRED, the FBI declined to comment on any “active investigation” but noted that it “is able to confirm we strive to increase impact on adversaries through partnerships as documented in our newly released FBI Cyber Strategy.” The AFP declined to comment.
About a month after his tip, Larsen says, US law enforcement had finished the legal process of requesting Thomson’s data from Google with a warrant. Late last month, Thomson was arrested by Australian police, who released a video of him being walked out of a suburban home in a Northface hoodie and sweatpants.
Neither Thomson nor Gaebler, the other alleged member of TeamPCP who was arrested, could be reached for comment.
Larsen was careful to note that Google’s undercover analyst inside of TeamPCP never engaged in any illegal hacking or even encouragement of the group’s breaches. “They were a fly on the wall, only saying enough to not be suspicious,” Larsen says. “There are guardrails around what we do.”
But Larsen also notes that his team’s work to actively foil TeamPCP’s hacking is part of a new shift within Google. The investigation, after all, kicked off around the same time as Google’s newly launched Cyber Disruption Unit, which has been officially tasked with taking a more aggressive approach to combating cybercrime and state-sponsored hacking.
“Google Threat Intelligence Group has put an emphasis on disruption. That’s one of our missions now,” Larsen says. “Writing reports can only be so useful. Taking action to protect users and customers—that is the next step.”

articles.title: Samsung is betting suppliers can handle conventional memory
articles.text:
Samsung could follow Micron by outsourcing DDR5 and SSD production to third parties to focus on more lucrative HBM and enterprise products — could SanDisk follow suit?
Samsung frees factory space for HBM by outsourcing DDR5 and SSD production
- Samsung is shifting additional DDR5 and SSD production to outside manufacturers
- The company needs internal factory space for advanced HBM production
- DDR5 module assembly remains simpler than advanced HBM packaging processes
Samsung Electronics is shifting all additional production of conventional memory modules onto outsourced partners going forward.
The company is directing capacity growth for DDR5 modules and SSDs toward external firms, reserving its in-house capacity for the more advanced HBM packaging process.
Industry sources say this reflects Samsung's mounting need to use scarce back-end capacity more efficiently.
A deliberate pivot toward outsourced capacity
“Samsung Electronics lacks space to expand existing back-end production lines needed to manufacture semiconductors for artificial intelligence (AI), so it is reallocating space and equipment at packaging plants in Cheonan and Onyang to advanced packaging lines, including HBM,” a person familiar with the matter said.
“The company has decided to handle most increases in conventional memory module production through outsourcing rather than expanding its own capacity.”
Samsung has reportedly pressed its outsourced semiconductor assembly and test partners to expand capacity for DDR5 modules and SSDs.
The company has even gone a step further by asking partners to accelerate capacity expansions that were already part of its existing plans.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Several partners are already scaling up in response, including Dreamtech, Hanyang Digitech, and SFA Semicon.
Dreamtech began mass producing DDR5 modules in India last November and approved further equipment investment in June.
Its Noida facility, previously used for smartphone circuit board assembly, will eventually reach an annual capacity of over 50 million units.
Hanyang Digitech has invested more than 31.5 billion won in 2026 so far to automate its existing memory module plant located in Vietnam.
SFA Semicon is relocating DDR5 testing and assembly equipment from Samsung's Onyang campus to a new site in the Philippines.
That transition begins in November, with a second phase following during the second quarter of 2027.
Limited space drives the broader manufacturing shift
Samsung's own capacity constraints stem partly from a new HBM plant under construction at its Onyang campus, valued at 6 trillion won.
That facility will take multiple years to finish, leaving little room for conventional module expansion in the meantime.
A separate $1.5 billion back-end processing plant is also under construction in Thai Nguyen Province of northern Vietnam.
That facility will handle testing for older memory types, including DDR4, low-power LPDDR4, NAND flash, and universal flash storage.
DDR5 modules require mounting prepackaged DRAM and NAND chips onto circuit boards using surface-mount technology.
That process remains considerably less complex than advanced packaging methods used for HBM, making outsourcing comparatively straightforward for partners.
Micron previously pursued a similar route, shifting conventional memory production externally while concentrating internal resources on higher-margin products.
Whether SanDisk eventually follows a comparable path remains uncertain given how differently each company's manufacturing footprint and product mix are currently structured.

articles.title: New California law will penalize influencers who don't disclose political ads | TechCrunch
articles.text:
New legislation signed by California Governor Gavin Newsom adds teeth to disclosure requirements for online influencers who are paid to post about politics.
The New York Times reports that California already required disclosure for influencers who post about state or local races — but when someone failed to disclose, there were no fines or criminal penalties. (Texas also requires disclosure for paid political content, and other states are considering similar regulations.)
Under the new bill, AB 1130, regulators can fine influencers up to $5,000 for each violation, and they can also refer them to law enforcement for potential misdemeanors.
According to the NYT, billionaire Tom Steyer, who unsuccessfully campaigned for the Democratic nomination for California governor earlier this year, paid dozens of influencers to post about his campaign online, and many of them did not initially disclose the payments.
Newsom signed the legislation as part of a broader package of bills that his office said will protect against potential election interference from President Donald Trump. The bill’s sponsor, Democratic Assemblyman Marc Berman, said that he introduced the bill after realizing there was “a bit of ambiguity about the [existing] law and how it’s enforced,”
