articles.title: A small but growing number of founders are betting on bringing people together offline | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Brynn Putnam and Tristan Walker have already done something that most founders only dream about: created companies so compelling that bigger outfits bought them. Putnam, a trained ballerina with a small chain of boutique studios, built the connected-fitness company Mirror and sold it to Lululemon for $500 million in cash less than three years later. Walker, who interned at Twitter while at Stanford business school, built the popular men’s grooming brand Walker & Company Brands, selling it five years later to Procter & Gamble for undisclosed terms (reportedly in the range of $20 million to $40 million).
That both of them are at it again is less surprising than the fact that their dramatically different new startups share the same north star: bringing people together, offline, in the same room.
Putnam’s new company, Board, which makes a 24-inch touchscreen table that recognizes physical game pieces as well as gestures, was built explicitly for a group sitting around it together rather than one person alone with a screen. Walker’s Heirloom is buying up and scaling fine-craft trade schools, starting with a leatherworking school in San Francisco founded by Hermès’s first American artisan-ambassador. (He’s also running Collaborative Holdings, a fund carved out by the venture firm Collaborative Fund built to give founders more time to build their businesses.)
On the surface, a game console and a leathercraft school don’t appear to have much in common. But both think there’s money is fostering the kind of connection that technology has eroded over the last couple of decades.
The timing isn’t accidental. In June of last year, the World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection formally classified loneliness as a defining global health challenge, estimating that one in six people worldwide are affected and linking the condition to roughly 870,000 deaths a year.
The opportunity to address that challenge is expanding, too, for those paying attention to it. In a Harris Poll survey sponsored by Marriott Bonvoy earlier this year, two-thirds of Americans said they were prioritizing experiences, like travel, over material purchases this year. (The same percentage said retail shopping today feels too generic, with all retailers looking and feeling the same.)
For now, East Coast entrepreneurs seem to be gravitating more naturally to the space, if it can be called that. Along with Putnam and Walker, two other founders whose newest businesses are focused on connection include Bonobos founder Andy Dunn and Audrey Gelman of the Wing.
Pie, Dunn’s now five-year-old company, has moved from friend-matching app to event-discovery tool to what he now calls a “social life operating system,” anchored by “Community Homes” — a permanent digital hub for recurring social groups like run clubs or watch parties.
Gelman tried this once before. Her last company, the Wing, built a business on bringing women together and folded during the pandemic amid accusations that it didn’t treat its own staff equitably. Now she’s found a different way to do something similar. Her current venture, the Six Bells Countryside Inn, an 11-room guesthouse in the Hudson Valley, hosts a monthly murder-mystery dinner where actors seed the crowd and, by dessert, someone turns up dead. The mystery itself is a little ridiculous by design, and so is the effect it has on guests. (According to a New York Times feature on the inn this summer, its visitors routinely linger in the bar past midnight, trading numbers with strangers.)
At one of TechCrunch’s recent StrictlyVC evening events, held in New York’s West Village, Putnam was candid about the fact that Mirror was built around her own life. She was pregnant with her first child, running brick-and-mortar fitness studios, and trying to bring that experience home through a screen using technology, as she put it, to work on “myself, my body, my fitness, my reflection.”
Board was built with the opposite in mind. Now a mother of five in a blended family — the household went from three people to seven — Putnam said she kept running into the same problem: no product on the market let people of wildly different ages and abilities play together. “How can we use tech to create a shared experience?” is the question she said drove the pivot. It wasn’t a “movement from digital to analog,” as she put it, “so much as how can we use tech to bring people together rather than take them apart.”
It’s why Board’s touchscreen recognizes the physical objects placed on it — a spaceship triggers an action, a knife performs a cut — instead of relying on the buttons and joysticks of a traditional controller; this way, a child and a grandparent can play the same game without a shared learning curve.
Walker had the same instinct, but his came from anxiety about what AI is doing to work and to community. He started Heirloom, he said, because he was worried about AI “stealing knowledge work” and pulling people away from each other. If he was going to build something after Walker & Company, he wanted it to bring people back together.
It’s an interesting bet. Speaking at the same StrictlyVC event, Walker said he believes the U.S. has forgotten how to transmit mastery, including leatherworking, watchmaking, and fragrance design. For 50 years, he argued, America has broken the chain from master to apprentice, offshoring production and stripping the prestige from manual skill to the point that apprenticeships became something people did when they couldn’t get into a four-year college.
Heirloom is a wager that that’s now reversing, and Walker had a number to back it up, telling a room full of founders and investors that roughly half of Gen Z and Gen Alpha say they don’t want a four-year degree at all. In fact, more than half of the capacity at Heirloom’s first location in San Francisco is currently filled not by career-changers or retirees but by young tech workers looking for what he calls a “phones-down creative outlet.”
So far, the dollars involved are relatively small for venture-backed startups. Putnam has raised $35 million from VCs for three-year-old Board. Pie has raised $24 million. Six Bells has raised roughly $3.8 million. Heirloom, founded 11 months ago, hasn’t disclosed its funding.
One exception is WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, whose new residential real estate venture Flow — marketed around the same premise of solving loneliness through physical space — has raised more than $450 million, largely from Andreessen Horowitz, dwarfing everyone else in this story combined.
Indeed, right now it’s unclear whether “togetherness” becomes its own sizable investment category. Getting strangers to show up for each other — as good as that may be for society — isn’t nearly as scalable as shipping software. What’s notable is who’s building these companies: Putnam, Walker, Dunn, Gelman, and Neumann have all built a real brand once before.
That makes it easier to raise capital and gives investors some confidence these are founders who know how to build something people actually buy. They’ve each guessed right about where the puck is headed once before. We’ll know more in another year or two whether enough customers follow along.

articles.title: Space, literacy, apparel: Test your business creativity with Edition 250 of our weekly quiz!
articles.text:
Space, literacy, apparel: Test your business creativity with Edition 250 of our weekly quiz!
This insightful feature from YourStory tests and strengthens your business acumen! Here are 5 questions to kick off this 250th quiz. Ready?
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 250th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.
What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?
Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.
Q1: Literacy
For millions of children, access to a classroom, teacher or book remains out of reach. What are some ways in which education can be brought to such underserved communities?
Q2: Circular economy
There are many sustainability solutions that deliver circular economy benefits at a small or local scale. How can such solutions be scaled up to the national level and beyond?
Q3: Accessories and design
Many consumers want beautiful, well-made accessories but are faced either with luxury imports or low-cost products. Where is the entrepreneurial opportunity here?
Q4: Ethnic wear
Children’s ethnic-wear clothes are often priced either at premium levels or low costs with low quality. How can better products be positioned here?
Q5: Space and data
Offering optical imaging solutions is a good entry path into the space-tech market. What kinds of new offerings can be layered on top of this foundation?
Answers!
Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!
A1: Literacy
There are a number of ways in which literacy can extend far beyond textbooks, such as Akash Tandon’s Pehchaan The Street School which brings education to slum children via volunteer teachers. Ngurang Meena and Reena founded The Street Library Initiative in Arunachal Pradesh, with 26 free-standing libraries across three districts.
Madhavi Shastri, K Srinivas Rao, and Shefali Rao, started the Food4Thought Foundation which has 622 libraries with books received from 425 donors. Read more here about Than Singh Ki Pathshala in Delhi, and Mission Ankur’s ways of teaching mathematics through songs and activities.
A2: Circular economy
Founded by Devang Kumar, Greenwave Circularity has developed a circular plastic recycling facility in Odisha. It can convert post-consumer bottle scrap into recycled resin and flakes for the FMCG industry.
The company’s joint venture partners include Jainarain Fabtech and Moon Beverage, a franchise bottler of Coca-Cola. Read more here about its solar power system, green-building certification, partnerships for scale, employment opportunities, and recent fundraise.
A3: Accessories
Founded by Sarthak Aggarwal, Vikram Jain, Karan Jain, and Shruti Aggarwal, Theater is positioned as a mass-premium brand for footwear, stockings, perfumes, and bags. It is priced for a generation that cares deeply about design but does not want to pay luxury prices.
“Consumers are willing to pay for products that have a point of view,” Jain observes. Read more here about its design-led options for consumers, and its recent fundraise from Prath Ventures.
A4: Ethnic wear
Founded by Rachana and Mihir Shah, Desi Tales makes pure cotton clothes with design details that avoid poking and itching. They can withstand children’s everyday wear and tear rather than being used only for festive occasions.
The “ethnic plus quirk” designs are partly handmade by women artisans in Gujarat and Rajasthan using Sanganeri block printing, and the rest is made through contract manufacturers. Read more here about how this D2C brand has served close to 40,000 customers over four years.
A5: Space and data
Founded by Awais Ahmed, Pixxel began with offerings in hyperspectral imaging, which captures information across many wavelengths of light. It is now expanding its focus to an earth intelligence software platform and sovereign earth observation systems.
Pixxel is scaling up its combination of software, datasets and satellite systems for commercial and government missions. Read more here about its recent fundraise, and its selection to lead India’s first public-private Earth observation constellation of 12 satellites under IN-SPACe.
YourStory has also published the pocketbook ‘Proverbs and Quotes for Entrepreneurs: A World of Inspiration for Startups’ as a creative and motivational guide for innovators.

articles.title: Un estudio explica por qué el radar de tramo es mucho más eficaz que el tradicional. Y tiene un sospechoso: el "efecto canguro"
articles.text:
No falla.
Aviso de radar, luces de freno y lo que era una carretera con tráfico denso pero fluido se convierte en una procesión de vehículos que viajan 20 km/h por debajo de la velocidad máxima permitida. Y de golpe, adiós al coche que te precede. Pisotón con el pie derecho y conductor que sale disparado. Hasta que llegue el próximo radar y la jugada se repita.
Es lo que se conoce en el argot más popular con el útil y cristalino nombre de: frenazo antes de un radar. O como han denominado en un estudio australiano con el más local: "efecto canguro". Un simpático nombre que define un comportamiento mucho menos simpático.
Y es que el conocido "efecto canguro" es un peligro.
Por favor, no pegues frenazos
Esa mención al "efecto canguro" llega de un metaanálisis australiano en el que se ha analizado el efecto de los radares a través 15 estudios en los que se ha analizado su impacto en la reducción de accidentes y otros cuatro estudios en los que el objetivo era el mismo pero centrados en los radares de tramo.
De ellos se concluye que los radares sí son efectivos. De hecho, se calcula que los radares redujeron en un 20% los accidentes allí donde estaban situados. Eso sí, el metaanálisis demostró que cuando se incorpora un radar de tramo a la vía, los accidentes se reducen en un 30% por lo que serían más eficaces. Pero ese no es el dato clave, el dato más interesante es que los accidentes mortales o con heridos graves se redujeron en un 56%.
Es decir, no sólo los radares de tramo proyectan mejores datos en los accidentes registrados, además los accidentes que se producen son menos graves. Y eso, aseguran, se debe en parte al "efecto canguro".
Según los datos del estudio, el radar tradicional es menos efectivo porque su eficacia se pierde conforme aumenta al distancia a dicho radar. Es decir, el conductor observaa el radar, frena y vuelve a acelerar con fuerza una vez pasado. Algo así como el salto del canguro cuando el animal toma impulso para llegar más lejos en su avance.
Estos mismos resultados son los que defienden en al DGT para incorporar más radares de tramo a las carreteras en detrimento de los tradicionales radares. Algunos de ellos, incluso, ya tienen 30 kilómetros en España. Además, en ocasiones se ha alertado que no sirve de nada ese "efecto canguro" porque la DGT habría ordenado poner radares móviles una vez superado el primer radar fijo. Una idea que la DGT ha desmentido a Xataka.

Desde hace varias décadas estas producciones se globalizaron gracias a que eran transmitidas en los canales locales en occidente y con el paso del tiempo se fueron integrando a los catálogos de las plataformas de streaming.
One Piece, Naruto y Bleach ostentan en los últimos años el título de “Big 3” por ser los tres animes más grandes de la última generación, sin embargo, en los años recientes nuevas historias han comenzado a alzar la mano para convertirse en el nuevo anime más exitoso de la historia.

Cada semana se publican los episodios a unas cuantas horas de diferencia de su transmisión en el país asiático. articles.title: Learning another language may be one of the best ways to keep your brain healthy
articles.text:
Learning another language is a highly complex mental activity. It requires people to remember words, distinguish unfamiliar sounds, recognize patterns, work out grammatical rules, and retrieve the right expression at the right moment. All of this happens while listening, interpreting, and preparing a response.
Could all this mental activity also help keep an aging brain healthier? Research suggests it can.
Concerns about memory and dementia can send aging adults looking for ways to exercise their brain and maintain cognitive function, whether it is solving crossword puzzles or playing a musical instrument. Language learning might not seem like the same kind of brain exercise, but it is a complex activity that engages several mental processes at once.
I am a linguist who studies language acquisition, use, and loss. My new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language, examines language and the mind across people’s lifespans.
Research increasingly suggests that language learning and bilingualism can offer cognitive benefits—including for older adults. Learning another language can also create opportunities for communication and social connection.
A workout for the brain
A person’s brain remains capable of change throughout their life. This ability to adapt in response to experience is known as neuroplasticity.
Learning unfamiliar sounds, vocabulary, and grammatical patterns requires the brain to form and strengthen connections. Language learning engages several mental processes at once, requiring people to absorb and retrieve information, notice when something does not work out, and adjust. This sustained mental effort makes language learning a particularly rich form of cognitive exercise.

articles.title: Japanese laptop maker crams an eight-core Ryzen AI 7 in a small body
articles.text:
Masters of Miniature delivers minuscule upgradable Ryzen AI laptop — Mouse has a 12.2-inch screen, weighs 981g, but ain't on sale outside Japan
Mouse X2 will not be sold outside Japan
- Mouse Computer has fitted Ryzen AI processors into a laptop weighing just 981g
- The X2 uses a 12.2-inch display with 1920 by 1200 resolution
- A free SODIMM slot allows memory expansion from 16 GB to 32 GB
Japanese electronics maker Mouse Computer has introduced a compact laptop called the X2, a compact notebook weighing 981g.
The device pairs a 12.2-inch display with AMD processors, offering configurations that scale from modest to genuinely capable performance.
The laptop frame measures 277.1 mm wide, 210.2 mm deep, and 19 mm tall, retaining a single unoccupied SODIMM slot for later RAM upgrades.
Specifications built around three AMD chip options
Buyers can choose between three distinct AMD APUs, each aimed at a different performance and price bracket for portable computing.
The base option, a Ryzen 5 216, combines two full Zen 4 cores with four smaller Zen 4c cores in a six-core layout, which should perform similarly to AMD's existing Ryzen 5 8540U based on available benchmark comparisons circulating online.
A step up brings the Ryzen AI 5 340, part of AMD's Krackan Point lineup, also arranged in a six-core configuration.
Multicore results suggest this chip lands close to Intel's Core Ultra 7 165H and edges past the Core Ultra 5 325.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The top configuration, a Ryzen AI 7 350, uses eight cores split evenly between four Zen 5 and four Zen 5c units, which approaches Intel's Core Ultra 9 185H in combined multi-threaded and synthetic benchmark scores, according to early comparisons.
The portable display panel runs at 1920 by 1200 resolution and reportedly covers 100% of the sRGB color gamut.
A 180-degree hinge, 60 Wh battery, and 500 GB NVMe SSD round out the internal hardware package.
Connectivity includes gigabit LAN, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5, USB Type-A ports, HDMI output, and a microSD card slot for storage expansion.
A 2 MP webcam with a privacy shutter supports Windows Hello, while Windows 11 Home ships preinstalled on every unit.
Battery life reaches roughly 12.5 hours during video playback and about 25 hours in idle mode, measured under JEITA 3.0 standards.
Pricing stays confined to the Japanese market for now
The Ryzen AI 5 variant, equipped with 16 GB of RAM and 500 GB of storage, costs ¥239,800, or roughly $1,545.
The higher Ryzen AI 7 configuration carries the same memory and storage allotment but costs ¥259,000, or about $1,670.
Sales of this device will begin sequentially from October, though the rollout remains confined to the Japanese market via the company’s online store for now.
The laptop is currently available in three colour options — Cosmo Blue, Frost Gold, and Pearl White.
Both versions ship with single-channel memory by default, though the empty SODIMM slot allows an upgrade path from 16GB to 32 GB.
A compatible 16 GB DDR5-5600 module currently retails for around $229 through Amazon's storefront.
Interested customers elsewhere would need to rely on import services to acquire a unit, adding cost and complexity to the process.

articles.title: The women forging India’s semiconductor push; How a perimenopause journey led to a midlife guide
articles.text:
The women forging India’s semiconductor push; How a perimenopause journey led to a midlife guide
A panel moderated by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, discussed the reasons why there are very few women leaders in the semiconductor industry and what it takes for women to rise to the top.
Dear Reader,
The closing day of SEMICON India 2026 brought to the fore ideas and proposals to give a push to collaboration and innovation and raise overall standards in the ecosystem.
India Semiconductor Mission CEO Amitesh Kumar Sinha has pitched a mega gathering that brings Semicon India, Bharat Electronics Manufacturing and Export Summit, and India Mobile Congress together in the same city and around the same location. Sinha believes this would help participants meet potential partners under one umbrella and better understand how semiconductors, electronics manufacturing, and telecom connect with each other.
This comes at a time when India looks to connect semiconductor manufacturing more closely with electronics, components, telecom and exports.
In other news, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade plans to come out with clearer guidelines and a policy framework within the next two to three months to address Quality Control Order-related hurdles faced by semiconductor and other deeptech companies. Quality Control Orders mandate that specified products comply with Indian standards, with the Bureau of Indian Standards overseeing certification.
In news from the world of global tech, just days after calling for a slowdown in AI development, Anthropic is planning to roll out a new AI model ahead of an expected IPO, Reuters reported. This comes in the wake of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra gaining momentum.
Lastly, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is expected to brief the United Nations Security Council next week at the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN General Assembly. The Security Council is to meet on Wednesday on AI and international security.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- The women forging India’s semiconductor push
- How a perimenopause journey led to a midlife guide
Here’s your trivia for today: Who is generally credited with the title of ‘father of the fabless industry’? (Scroll down for the answer)
Semicon India 2026
The women forging India’s semiconductor push
A panel moderated by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, discussed the reasons why there are so few women leaders in the semiconductor industry and what it takes for women to rise to the top.
The panellists were Alpa Sood, Country Manager at Teradyne India; Usha Gogineni, Director of Technology Development at Micron; Radhika Viswanathan, Chief Operating Officer at Applied Materials India; Malini Narayanamoorthi, President of Renesas India and Vice President at Renesas Electronics; and Lavanya S, Senior Department Manager at Tata Electronics.
Key takeaways:
- Senior women executives from Teradyne, Micron, Applied Materials, Renesas, and Tata Electronics suggested ways to close the leadership gap in the industry, through mentorship networks, flexible career paths, and visible role models.
- Alpa, who leads Teradyne's India business, said the job takes resilience first, and it is fine to cry it out as long as you show up the next day with a smile. Usha of Micron emphasised the importance of adaptability, curiosity, and a willingness to try different things. Meanwhile, Radhika of Applied Materials raised a subtle problem: women often get less feedback than men because male managers worry they will take it personally, a point she said Indra Nooyi's autobiography makes well.
- Malini built her career in applications engineering, chose breadth over depth, and returned to India about five years ago to build and scale Renesas’ design team. Lavanya, who worked at TSMC in Taiwan before joining Tata Electronics to help bring up India's first fab, said, the way forward, regardless of gender, is to take on the hardest projects early.
Books
How a perimenopause journey led to a midlife guide
In Women-O-Pause, actor and author Lenaa Kumar brings together her personal experience, research and expert perspectives to make conversations around perimenopause and menopause more accessible.
Key takeaways:
- Actor Lenaa Kumar did not set out to write a book on menopause. She began writing to make sense of a life stage that can leave women questioning their bodies, identities and sense of self. The physical, mental and, “energy-wise” unravelling became the starting point of an obsessive year of research, eventually leading to Women-O-Pause.
- Women-O-Pause is a midlife guide based on her understanding that every human being is a composite of consciousness, energy, mind and body. In the book, Lenaa distinguishes between the outward-facing energy women have been conditioned to operate in and what she calls feminine energy—receptive, intuitive, restorative.
- The book is written in a simple and accessible language, so that the information reaches everyone. The idea is to make sure the average woman, with no science or medical background, can understand it easily.
News & updates
- AI evaluation: Anthropic is to partner with Accenture for an independent evaluation of its frontier AI models, with the companies each committing at least $1 billion over the next five years to build capacity for the work.
- AI hacks: Google’s Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities. The hacks occurred in May during a cybersecurity test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.
Who is generally credited with the title of ‘father of the fabless industry’?
Answer: Gordon A. Campbell

articles.title: El mayor acierto de las gafas de las Ray-Ban Meta se ha convertido en su problema. Por eso el futuro pasa por quitarles la cámara
articles.text:
Hoy en día, al parecer, en una primera cita también hay que fijarse en las gafas del otro. Wired ha reunido varios testimonios de mujeres que descubrieron que su cita llevaba unas Ray-Ban Meta y que, en algunos casos, la había estado grabando. Todas dicen sentirse igual: invadidas y descartando a su cita de inmediato.
Al mismo tiempo, alguien ha creado la aplicación 'ZuckOff', que busca señales Bluetooth para avisarte de que hay unas gafas de Meta cerca.
Creo que es fácil leer estas noticias como un rechazo a la tecnología, pero nadie rechaza que alguien lleve un pequeño ordenador en la cara. Lo que se rechaza es un reparto concreto: quien lleva las gafas se queda con las ventajas y el riesgo lo asumen quienes están delante. Esas personas tienen que saber qué son, dónde está la cámara y si el pilotito está encendido. No han comprado nada, pero les toca apechugar y estar alerta.
Hay una regla bastante fiable para saber qué tecnologías acaban normalizándose: cuando el coste lo paga quien la use, se termina aceptando. Con el Walkman ocurrió: parecía de maleducados aislarse en ciertos entornos con unos auriculares, pero el aislado era uno mismo. Con los primeros manos libres de principios de siglo pasó algo similar: ver a alguien hablando solo por la calle daba risa, pero el "ridículo" era de quien lo hacía. Hoy a nadie le llama la atención ver a alguien hablando con unos auriculares inalámbricos puestos.
Las gafas con cámara rompen esa regla porque el coste recae en otros. Por eso se están vendiendo cada vez mejor pero al mismo tiempo empieza a haber un debate sobre lo molestas que pueden resultar.
Ahí aparece Luna, el nombre en clave de unas próximas gafas de Meta que no llevan cámara. Sí mantendrían altavoces, micrófonos y asistente. Reuters pronostica una presentación en los próximos días. Tiene su lógica porque hay gente que quiere hablar con una IA sin cargar con el estigma, y hay sitios donde el modelo con cámara ya no puede entrar. Algunos espacios no aceptan estas gafas.
Sin la cámara, las gafas vuelven a funcionar como el Walkman: si hablar con tus gafas queda raro, el que queda raro eres tú, y nadie más se juega nada. Además, se quedan con lo que la mayoría hace a diario con ellas: escuchar música y podcasts, atender llamadas y hacer alguna pregunta en voz alta.
Hacer fotos desde la altura de nuestros ojos es una maravilla, sobre todo para generar recuerdos cotidianos inmediatos y desde nuestra perspectiva habitual. He probado casi todos los modelos de gafas de Meta (además, el concepto me convenció desde el principio) y esa es sin duda su ventaja principal. Pero fuera de nuestros círculos de confianza, ir por el mundo con la cámara en la montura suele ser lo más inquietante.
Nuestro miedo es sobre todo visual. La cámara nos asusta porque es un ojo, y un ojo se ve. En cambio, llevamos quince años con micrófonos en el bolsillo y ni nos acordamos de ellos. Unas gafas con seis micros nos inquietan mucho menos que una sola cámara, aunque a menudo lo que decimos es mucho más íntimo y delicado que lo que se ve.
Esta categoría va a tener que aprender algo que Meta quiso evitar: que se note qué gafas no pueden grabar. Que sea fácil darse cuenta de que son unas gafas de Meta pero aún más fácil darse cuenta de que son las que no tienen cámara. Si lo consigue, el camino estará despejado. Cuando se hable de las gafas que han marcado la década de los 20s, posiblemente no serán las que prometían ver por nosotros. Tiene pinta de que aceptaremos que un dispositivo nos escuche a todas horas (lo que los nuevos Apple Watch plantean, por cierto) antes que dejarle mirar a quien tenemos delante.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 vs Honor Magic V6 : comment choisir le meilleur smartphone pliable Android ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une chose est sûre, le duel s’annonce palpitant. Fraîchement sorti des usines Samsung, le Galaxy Z Fold 8 écope d’un 8/10 « Coup de cœur » de la part de la rédaction, malgré son prix d’entrée de 1 999 euros. Le Honor Magic V6 repart lui aussi avec un 8/10, mais peut aujourd’hui se retrouver à des tarifs un peu plus abordables (il est sorti au début de l’été).
Quel est le meilleur smartphone des deux ? Réponse à l’issue de ce comparatif.
Les fiches techniques des Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 et Honor Magic V6
| Modèle | Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | Honor Magic V6 | 
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions | 123,9 mm x 161,4 mm x 4,5 mm | 145,6 mm x 156,7 mm x 4,0 mm | 
| Interface constructeur | One UI | MagicOS | 
| Taille de l’écran | 7,6, 5,5 pouces | 7,95 pouces | 
| Définition | 2448 x 1848 pixels | 2352 x 2172 pixels | 
| Densité de pixels | 403 ppp | 403 ppp | 
| Technologie | AMOLED | AMOLED | 
| SoC | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | 
| Puce graphique | Adreno 840 | Adreno 840 | 
| Stockage interne | 256, 512, 1024 Go | 512 Go | 
| Appareil photo (dorsal) | Capteur 1 : 50 Capteur 2 : 50 Mp | Capteur 1 : 50 Capteur 2 : 64 Capteur 3 : 50 Mp | 
| Capteur photo frontal | 10 Mp | 20 Mp | 
| Définition enregistrement vidéo | 4K @ 60 fps | 4K @ 60 fps | 
| Wi-fi | Wi-Fi 7 (be) | Wi-Fi 7 (be) | 
| Bluetooth | 6.0 | 6.0 | 
| 5G | Oui | Oui | 
| NFC | Oui | Oui | 
| Capteur d’empreintes | latéral | latéral | 
| Type de connecteur | USB Type-C | USB Type-C | 
| Capacité de la batterie | 4800 mAh | 6660 mAh | 
| Poids | 201 g | 219 g | 
| Couleurs | Blanc, Gris | Noir, Blanc, Rouge | 
|  | Fiche produit Voir le test | Fiche produit Voir le test | 
Un nouveau format qui plait beaucoup
Samsung bouleverse la formule des smartphones pliants avec son nouveau Fold 8, qui adopte un format dit « passeport », plus large que long. Particulièrement compact, il se glisse facilement dans un sac ou une poche. Cela étant, il reste plus épais que son concurrent direct (quand bien même ses capteurs photo sont particulièrement proéminents).
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quels sont les meilleurs smartphones pliables en 2026 ? Samsung Galaxy Z, Honor Magic V, Motorola Razr… le comparatif
            
Autant l’écrire : le Galaxy Z Fold 8 est un coup de cœur. L’avenir nous dira si c’est simplement l’attrait de la nouveauté, ou si le format wide est vraiment viable.
Dans tous les cas, le mobile de Samsung s’affiche dans un design bien plus consensuel que son concurrent le Honor Magic V6 qui, vous l’avez remarqué, a un côté bling-bling assumé. C’est un style ; on aime ou pas. Reste que le V6 n’a rien à envier à son rival sur des aspects comme la robustesse de la charnière, la pliure de l’écran ou même la résistance globale, avec sa certification IP68/69. En face, le Fold 8 fait moins bien avec une certification IP48 qui indique une moins bonne résistance face aux poussières et petites particules, notamment. Enfin, précisons que le Honor Magic V6 est compatible avec l’usage d’un stylet (vendu séparément).
Samsung impressionne avec son écran large
C’est ici que le duel devient technique et fascinant. Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 propose une dalle interne de 7,6 pouces au format 4:3, ce qui fait une vraie différence pour la lecture ou le visionnage de vidéos en mode horizontal. Ses caractéristiques sont impressionnantes : une luminosité maximale de 3000 nits en HDR, mais il souffre d’une calibration couleur perfectible avec un Delta E moyen de 6,55 en HDR. Son écran externe de 5,5 pouces affiche 1390 nits en SDR et 2930 nits en HDR, avec une température moyenne de 6822 K – ce qui est un peu froid, par défaut.
Le Honor Magic V6, lui, déploie une dalle interne plus vaste de 7,95 pouces (2352 x 2172 pixels) et une dalle externe de 6,52 pouces. Sur le plan de la précision, le Honor est plus stable avec une température moyenne excellente de 6481 K sur l’écran interne, bien qu’il peine à atteindre ses promesses de luminosité : il plafonne à 1200 nits en SDR comme en HDR sur la dalle interne, ce qui peut nuire à la lisibilité en plein soleil malgré un pic théorique promis de 5000 nits. Enfin, l’écran du Galaxy est un peu plus généreux en matière de couverture colorimétrique, avec un DCI-P3 couvert à 87 %, contre 83 % pour son rival.
D’excellentes interfaces
Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 s’appuie sur One UI 9 (Android 17), une interface qui s’est imposée comme une référence pour le multitâche sur grands écrans. Sa force réside dans la fluidité des interactions et une gestion des fenêtres parfaitement optimisée pour le format novateur de l’appareil. Pour les utilisateurs avancés, Samsung propose la possibilité d’afficher trois applications simultanément en mode horizontal, une disposition bien plus intuitive et équilibrée que sur les modèles Ultra.
L’intégration des fonctions Galaxy AI est omniprésente, notamment pour la retouche photo, et l’intelligence artificielle Gemini est profondément ancrée dans le système pour l’assistance quotidienne. Samsung garantit enfin une longévité exceptionnelle avec 7 ans de mises à jour Android et de sécurité. Un point de friction notable relevé dans notre test reste l’absence du Flex Mode, sacrifié ici pour garantir une ouverture fluide de la charnière.
À l’opposé, le Honor Magic V6 utilise MagicOS 10 (Android 16), une interface qui mise davantage sur l’esthétique et la personnalisation. Le constructeur propose des options de transparence pour les widgets et le volet de contrôle rapide, clairement inspirées des codes visuels d’iOS. Bien qu’Honor offre également un suivi logiciel de 7 ans, son approche de l’IA est plus discrète, avec une liste de fonctions dédiées mais une intégration moins poussée que chez son concurrent. Une particularité notable est la volonté d’Honor d’intégrer l’écosystème Apple, bien que le transfert de fichiers vers iPhone nécessite encore l’installation d’une application tierce.
Des performances au coude à coude… sur le papier
Les deux appareils sont propulsés par le processeur Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, mais leur gestion diffère. Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 est une machine fluide mais « bridée » pour limiter la chaleur, tournant souvent à 80 % de ses capacités de CPU. Il gère sans problème Genshin Impact à 60 FPS en maximum, mais peut atteindre 47 °C en stress test. Le Honor Magic V6 est plus capricieux, et nous avons rencontré des soucis avec plusieurs unités de test. Nos benchmarks montrent des incohérences selon les lots de production, avec des modèles parfois « bridés » et d’autres montrant une puissance de pointe en mode Performance (gain de 20 % de puissance). En mode Équilibré, il est très stable, mais il peut souffrir de throttling et de chutes de performance brutales toutes les 10 minutes en usage intensif.
Bref, il semble que le Galaxy s’en sorte de manière un peu plus stable, et fiable, dans l’ensemble.
Deux bons photophones
Les smartphones pliants sont traditionnellement des photophones plus modestes que les flagships classiques (ils ont des impératifs d’épaisseur à respecter). Cela étant, Samsung comme Honor proposent pourtant de très bons résultats en photo. Cela étant, on préfère vous avertir : seul le Magic offre un téléobjectif.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
- Grand-angle : 50 Mpx, f/1.8, OIS
- Ultra grand-angle : 50 Mpx, f/1.9
- Selfie : 10 Mpx + 10 Mpx, f/1.9
Honor Magic V6
- Grand-angle 50 Mpx, f/1.6, OIS
- Ultra grand-angle : 50 Mpx, f/2.2
- Téléobjectif 3x : 64 Mpx, f/2.5
- Selfie : 20 Mpx + 20 Mpx, f/2.2
Le capteur grand-angle du Honor Magic V6 se distingue par une gestion du contraste très maîtrisée et une netteté remarquable de jour, offrant une précision sur les détails du visage en mode portrait que le Samsung peut parfois manquer. À l’inverse, le module principal du Galaxy Z Fold 8 propose une dynamique étendue et des couleurs saturées mais naturelles, évitant les pièges chromatiques courants. Dans l’ensemble, le Honor semble toutefois offrir un meilleur piqué.
En ce qui concerne l’ultra grand-angle, les deux modèles se confrontent aux limites physiques de cette optique en basse lumière, produisant des images plus molles et bruitées dès que la luminosité faiblit. Cela étant, le Galaxy Z Fold 8 offre des rendus de jour tout à fait honorables qui ne souffrent pas de décalage de qualité par rapport au capteur principal, offrant une meilleure continuité visuelle.
Enfin, la partie zoom marque la différence la plus nette entre les deux appareils : le Honor Magic V6 intègre un véritable téléobjectif x3 optique offrant une réelle polyvalence, malgré un manque de cohérence colorimétrique notable avec le grand-angle. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 ne propose qu’un zoom x2 purement numérique basé sur un recadrage du capteur principal, ce qui garantit une parfaite cohérence chromatique sur chaque cliché au détriment de la profondeur de champ optique. Naturellement, le Honor conserve pour sa part une bien meilleure finesse d’affichage en raison de sa résolution supérieure.
L’autonomie pose toujours souci
Le Honor Magic V6 est le champion de l’endurance grâce à sa batterie colossale de 6660 mAh enrichie de 25 % en silicium-carbone. Il permet d’atteindre deux jours d’autonomie en usage modéré et résiste 16 heures en test PCMark (en mode fermé). Sa charge rapide est de 80 W (nécessitant un chargeur adapté), capable de charger 81 % en 30 minutes.
En face, le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 embarque une batterie de 4800 mAh bien plus modeste, mais non moins optimisée. Il assure une journée et demi d’utilisation active et propose une charge de 45 W, qui permet de récupérer 63 % de batterie en 15 minutes.
D’après les tests standardisés de GSMArena, le Honor Magic V6 s’en tire mieux, avec 15h21 d’autonomie contre 13h59 pour son concurrent au format passeport.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ou Honor Magic V6 : lequel choisir ?
On l’avait prévu : le duel est effectivement très serré, et il nous faut prendre un peu de hauteur pour voir émerger un vainqueur assez net. D’après nous, aujourd’hui, le Honor Magic V6 est objectivement le meilleur smartphone pliant des deux. Il est plus robuste, offre une meilleure autonomie, et surtout une bien meilleure expérience en photographie.
Cela étant, le Fold 8 impressionne avec son nouveau format compact, qui offre une expérience de navigation inédite qui, à elle seule, pourrait suffire à vous faire craquer. Il dispose par ailleurs des meilleurs écrans, de la meilleure interface, et des performances les plus stables.
Maintenant, on est face à deux smartphones qui ne sont pas donnés, et le prix de l’un ou de l’autre pourrait achever d’aiguiller votre choix.

articles.title: AMD Claims EPYC "Venice" Beats NVIDIA Vera by 2.24x in New White Paper
articles.text:
Saturday, September 19th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
AMD Claims EPYC "Venice" Beats NVIDIA Vera by 2.24x in New White Paper
AMD has published a white paper on its 6th Gen EPYC 9006 "Venice" server CPUs, and it takes direct aim at NVIDIA's Vera. These are first-party figures from AMD, so it is important to be cautious about their validity. In SPECrate 2026 Integer, AMD says the 256-core EPYC 9996 delivers 2.24 times the platform-level performance of an 88-core Vera system, while a 96-core, high-frequency Venice chip is claimed to be 1.2 times faster per core. Against Intel's Xeon 6980P, AMD reports gains of 2.4x to 3.7x in server-side Java, OpenSSL, MongoDB, Redis, NGINX and transaction processing, and up to 3.13x in HPC tests like GROMACS. Neither AMD nor NVIDIA can publish official SPEC results yet, so all of it is estimated. 
The Vera figures come from NVIDIA's own white paper, and the 96-core part is an EPYC 9996 with several of its cores turned off. The per-subtest results also used GCC 16.1 on the AMD side against GCC 15.2 for NVIDIA, which Tom's Hardware notes is not best practice. The 2.24x figure compares a 512-thread flagship with Vera's 176 threads, so it is not a like-for-like matchup. AMD says Venice is in production, with major OEM platforms on track to launch and cloud providers starting deployments later this year. It's likely we will only get a real answer once independent reviewers get both chips on the same test bench.

articles.title: Collapse of mainstream optical drive supply kills high-end CD players — PS Audio and Naim halt production as component costs double
articles.text:
Collapse of mainstream optical drive supply kills high-end CD players — PS Audio and Naim halt production as component costs double
What would happen if the optical drive on your Hi-Fi player fails and replacements are no longer available?
Many audiophiles still prefer physical media like CDs and vinyl over streaming, especially those who want to own their music, which is why we’re seeing a resurgence in sales for these media. However, one major concern hitting some Hi-Fi brands is the lack of optical drives built for mainstream computers, which has caused the supply chain for key components to dry up. According to Headphonesty, Naim’s Uniti Star and PS Audio’s PMG Super Audio CD Transport have ended production because their suppliers no longer make the optical hardware these units need.
Unfortunately, both companies cannot easily find replacements for these out-of-production components. “The drives appropriate for a PMG are no longer available,” PS Audio CEO Paul McGowan said in the company forum. He also added that building its own optical disc reader is beyond PS Audio’s capabilities, saying that its expertise is in electronics and software. It’s also the same problem that Naim is facing, with one commenter in its own forum saying that it assembles components instead of manufacturing them from raw parts and materials.
PS Audio’s problems began in June 2024, when D&M Holdings, which owns Denon and Marantz, said that it would stop taking orders for its SACD/CD mechanism by the end of the following month. This meant that the company needed to place its final order before the deadline, with costs doubling as other brands scrambled to build their stockpiles. This was probably because D&M was the only company producing and selling that particular component to third parties. McGowan stated that Marantz has ended production of its SACD/CD drives and that PS Audio has completely bought out the company’s last remaining inventory.
While it’s unclear which supplier Naim used for its Uniti Star Streaming Amplifier, it’s been said that the company did consider an alternative supplier for its optical drives. Unfortunately, this is not an easy swap in the production line, as these optical media readers are often built as an assembly, meaning installing a different model requires new control codes and mechanical tweaks inside these units. As Naim was considering how to integrate this substitute drive into its existing Uniti Star product, the alternative ceased production as well.
You can still buy Hi-Fi CD players and transports today, but these units from Naim and PS Audio are already out of stock if you want them brand new. Thankfully, the two companies keep some components in their inventory for repairs, so existing owners don’t have to worry about getting their expensive systems bricked just because the optical readers on their devices have failed.

 Harmonic Masking and Vinyl "Warmth"The interaction between the RIAA curve and the inherent distortion of vinyl playback changes the tonal perception of music: 
 A fundamental tone at 40 Hz gets boosted significantly by the RIAA playback preamp.
 Its 2nd harmonic (80 Hz) and 3rd harmonic (120 Hz) are also amplified, though slightly less so because the curve begins to flatten out.
 This amplification of low-frequency harmonics adds a psychoacoustic sense of fullness, richness, and "warmth" that listeners often associate with analog audio.

articles.title: Broken Sword creator explains why he’s choosing humans over AI to develop 2 remake
articles.text:
Broken Sword creator chose human artists over AI for all 55,000 new frames of animation in the upcoming 2 remake — 'People are going to seek out human-crafted art'
The human touch
Charles Cecil wants to make one thing clear: “I'm not anti-AI.”
The veteran British developer behind the legendary 1996 point-and-click game Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars speaks to TechRadar about AI's divisive role in modern game development - and, in particular, how it was used in the upcoming remake of the sequel, Broken Sword - The Smoking Mirror: Reforged, due out in 2027.
The original, a commercial success selling 759,000 copies, sees American tourist George Stobbart team up with freelance journalist Nicole Collard to track a mysterious Mayan stone across Paris, London, and Central America. This remake doesn't use AI, and, according to Cecil, there's a very good reason for that.
AI don’t think so
“I think AI has its place,” Cecil says. “It's just not relevant in our games because we want human animation, human characterization and human expression, and that's much better done by humans.”
A perfect example of that lies in the game's hand-drawn art, all of it redone for Broken Sword - The Smoking Mirror: Reforged.
This hugely labor-intensive process encompassed roughly 55,000 frames of animation, more than the 30,000 of Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars’ 2024 remake.
“George opens the newspaper and kind of just glances at the screen,” says Cecil, referring to the actions of the game's protagonist in an early scene. “He's looking at the viewer, and that's what human beings do. That is not something that AI can do.”
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In low-res, eyes were just dots on a face. In high-res, eyes are windows to the soul and therefore have to be animated with precision and intent. Where applicable, artists were free to add flourishes, using their own interpretation to fill in the gaps.
For instance, the painting of Professor Oubier hanging on the wall in the rapidly burning study was always too pixelated to see clearly. Now, however, you can make out exactly what he looks like in 4K, at 36 times the original resolution, all while a visibly uncomfortable George jostles his rope bindings.
Developer Revolution Software didn't stop there. The team redrew scores of items that never really made much sense. Take the poison dart, which now looks less like a playing dart and more like something shot out of a blowpipe.
Human revolution
Despite the decision to abstain from AI use for the most part, it wasn't entirely absent. AI was used for the initial round of upscaling before artists added detail by hand, with backgrounds scanned as black-and-white layouts for them to build on using the originals as references. AI was more of a tool than a creative device.
“We experimented with AI for the first one, and we used AI to upscale and then redraw the characters. And as I say, it can upscale, but it can't put any character in.”
That's largely thanks to the luxury of time. The first game needed to be made in a year or risk cancellation. Revolution Software sprinted to the finish line, but made a few shortcuts along the way.
One oversight was 40 voice lines that were recorded and packaged in the game's files but never used. Now, in Broken Sword - The Smoking Mirror: Reforged, fans can finally hear them (one line involves George asking the Parisian waiter about the tequila worm in his pocket).
Another infamous example occurs in the Game Boy Advance version. “You have a choice to go to Spain or Syria,” says Cecil. “If you do one, you can finish the game, and it's fine. If you do the other, it takes you there, but you can't then finish. There's a bug that doesn't allow you to finish…It's an awful, awful bug. I mean, it's absolutely shocking.”
An AI might have spotted such mistakes, but then again, you could argue mistakes are what give art humanity. If nothing else, they make for a great story.
But the remake is far from a bug-fixing exercise. Instead, it's an opportunity to make the game better. Where most remasters seek to preserve the subject, Broken Sword - The Smoking Mirror: Reforged is almost an act of excavation.
“All of these things we now have the time to do,” says Cecil. “Because what Revolution has done for the last 15 years is we've self-published all our games. And I can decide when we’re going to spend a little bit more time getting this, right? Is it worth it?”
The devs found time to add features, too, like a new three-tier hint system that actively monitors your progress and feeds you steadily more obvious tips so you're not stuck for too long. The final tip tells you outright what to do. Thankfully, purists can turn it off.
Meanwhile, Nintendo Switch 2 players get four different control schemes: touchscreen, gamepad, one Joy-Con 2 detached and used as a mouse, or a versatile combination of everything.
Plus, there’s something Cecil has personally wanted to add for 30 years: a beautiful, detailed map of Paris. This is used to aid player navigation instead of having them rely on clunky icons. With everything in the game, these feel like choices made by humans, not AI.
“We've really gone out of our way to produce something that, in my view, is completely future-proof, because people were playing the first one 30 years ago, and millions and millions of people have played that game. And my ambition is that in 20 years' time, a fourth generation will be playing again.”
“Going forward,” he continues, “people are going to seek out human-crafted art. You know, there's going to be that sense, because obviously we all have a human connection with each other.”

articles.title: Juegos gratis de la semana en Epic Games Store: cómo descargar los 3 títulos
articles.text:
Epic Games ofrece tres títulos gratuitos: Aniimo, Shogun Showdown y Mindcop. Este último también está disponible para celulares.
Para acceder a estos juegos, basta con ingresar a Epic Games y buscar cada título en la tienda.
PUBLICIDAD
De qué tratan estos juegos gratuitos de Epic Games
Aniimo es un RPG de mundo abierto centrado en la captura de criaturas. Los jugadores recorren el continente de Idyll para encontrar, capturar y entrenar a los Aniimo, que pueden evolucionar según las condiciones del entorno.
Una de sus mecánicas principales permite fusionarse con estas criaturas para utilizar sus habilidades en combates, acertijos y desplazamientos por el mapa. También incluye desafíos en tiempo real y opciones multijugador.
Shogun Showdown combina combates por turnos, construcción de mazos y elementos roguelike.
El objetivo es posicionarse en el escenario y elegir el momento indicado para atacar, mientras se mejoran fichas de habilidades y se crean combinaciones.
Cada partida permite desbloquear nuevos personajes, ataques y destrezas antes de enfrentar al shogun, en un universo inspirado en Japón y con gráficos de estilo pixel art.
PUBLICIDAD
Por su parte, Mindcop es una aventura policial no lineal en la que el jugador debe resolver un asesinato en la aldea de Campamento Merrylin Crater.
El protagonista cuenta con cinco días para identificar al culpable entre los habitantes del lugar y puede ingresar en las mentes de los sospechosos mediante rompecabezas en tiempo real para obtener pistas, detectar mentiras y decidir qué líneas de investigación seguir.

Steam ofrece Diablo IV, Sea of Thieves y más juegos gratis
Steam ofrece siete juegos y un contenido adicional gratuitos para PC por tiempo limitado. La promoción incluye Deadshot, Sea of Thieves: 2026 Edition, el paquete Dying Light: The Beast - Discharge Weapon Pack, Space Menace, Diablo IV, Crystal Crisis, Last Flag y Jump Space.
PUBLICIDAD
Deadshot, Space Menace y Crystal Crisis aparecen con la etiqueta “Free to Keep”, por lo que pueden añadirse a la biblioteca de forma permanente mientras la oferta siga disponible.
En tanto, Sea of Thieves: 2026 Edition, Diablo IV, Last Flag y Jump Space figuran como “Play for Free”. La selección también incluye Dying Light: The Beast - Discharge Weapon Pack, un contenido adicional para Dying Light: The Beast y no un juego independiente.}
Para obtener los títulos identificados como “Free to Keep”, hay que ingresar a la página de cada producto en Steam y seleccionar la opción para instalarlo o añadirlo a la biblioteca antes de la fecha límite.
PUBLICIDAD
Una vez reclamados durante el período de promoción, Deadshot, Space Menace y Crystal Crisis quedarán asociados a la cuenta del usuario. La disponibilidad puede variar según la región y las condiciones indicadas en la tienda digital.
En el caso de Sea of Thieves: 2026 Edition, Diablo IV, Last Flag y Jump Space, Steam los presenta como pruebas gratuitas. Esto significa que el acceso está limitado al período establecido por cada promoción y no implica necesariamente que el juego quede incorporado de forma permanente a la biblioteca.
El paquete Dying Light: The Beast - Discharge Weapon Pack también debe reclamarse desde su página en Steam. Al tratarse de contenido adicional, requiere contar con Dying Light: The Beast para poder utilizarlo.

articles.title: Rings around a tiny body have changed over the past decade
articles.text:
For decades, astronomers thought rings were something only giant planets had. That changed in 2013, when a small, dark body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus passed in front of a star and blinked twice on either side of the main event, revealing two narrow rings around an object barely 250 kilometers across. “It was a surprise,” says Pablo Santos-Sanz, an astronomer at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Granada, Spain. Ever since, the question has been what such rings are made of and how long they can last.
In a recent study, Santos-Sanz and his colleagues used the James Webb Space Telescope to watch the same body, now known as Chariklo, pass in front of a background star again. They found one of its rings had grown denser and the other had almost vanished. We don’t know exactly why.
Shadowing a star
The technique behind the observation is simple. “We predict when a Solar System object passes in front of a star,” Santos-Sanz said. The starlight dims for a moment, and the shape of that dip reveals the size, shape, and surroundings of the object that caused it. “This is particularly challenging for minor bodies, and more challenging for distant minor bodies,” he said.
The difficulty is that the target’s silhouette on the sky is minuscule, and knowing when it will cross a particular star requires very precise positioning data for both. Still, in 2013, we used ground telescopes to discern Chariklo’s two rings, C1R and C2R. These sat 390 and 405 kilometers from its center and were only a few kilometers wide and about 7 kilometers apart.
Doing this with a space-based telescope, though, makes lining things up considerably harder. JWST sits at the L2 Lagrange point, and controllers need to nudge the telescope every few weeks to keep its orbit stable. “It’s a kind of tricky task,” Santos-Sanz said. His team identified a possible Chariklo occultation in August 2022 and redid the prediction every week. Between the first prediction and one of the last, the projected line of sight shifted by about 110 kilometers, which was enough to move it off the body entirely. Unfortunately, JWST requires observations like this to be planned at least 14 days in advance.
“We did this maybe a bit blindly, because we didn’t know exactly where the line of sight was,” Santos-Sanz said. “I’m going to move one of the biggest, best telescopes in space, and we don’t know if finally we will catch this or not.” But it all worked out.
The occultation came on October 18, 2022. The reconstructed geometry shows JWST’s sightline to the background star skimmed 7.4 kilometers above Chariklo’s surface, missing the body but catching its rings.
The ring that thickened
JWST recorded the event simultaneously in two near-infrared bands, at 1.5 and 3.2 micrometers, which made it the first time anyone has caught a minor body’s rings in a band beyond three micrometers—a range Earth’s atmosphere puts out of reach for ground telescopes.
The inner ring showed up unmistakably, with abrupt, distinct edges, but it was much darker than before. Averaged over roughly 10 previous ground-based occultations, C1R’s normal opacity (the fraction of starlight it blocks) sat at 0.303. JWST measured it at 0.431. “We didn’t believe it at the beginning, so we fought a lot with the data,” Santos-Sanz said.
The most straightforward explanation was geometry. Rings are not always uniform, and JWST might simply have cut through a denser clump. To rule this scenario out, the team built a lumpy ring model and ran 10 million simulated occultations. Reproducing an opacity as high as JWST recorded came out at a roughly 1 in a 1,000 chance at 1.5 micrometers, and 4 in 100,000 at 3.2 micrometers for a single measurement. The telescope caught the ring twice, going in and coming out, which made the odds even smaller than that.
Santos-Sanz concluded that the inner ring most likely got thicker. At the same time, the outer ring did the opposite.
The ring that faded
C2R barely registered at 1.5 micrometers and did not appear at all at 3.2, even though the telescope was recording the same stretch of ring in both bands at the same instant. “At the beginning we didn’t even see the outer ring in the light curve,” Santos-Sanz said. “We had to use models. It was really barely visible, so we said, ‘What is happening here?’”
The team came up with two possible explanations. The first is that JWST, looking at wavelengths where almost no occultation has ever been recorded, is simply seeing grains that scatter light differently in the infrared. The other is that the rings really have physically changed. Santos-Sanz argues radiative transfer models point toward the latter. The older visible-light observations were consistent with a mixture of ice and silicates, but once the JWST data points are added, no combination of materials and grain sizes could explain what the telescope has seen.
“We are witnessing a real evolution of the rings with time,” Santos-Sanz said. “Of course it is not a certainty, but for me it is the preferred explanation.” What’s more, this evolution most likely was not just the material from the fading outer ring migrating inward to the inner ring. Measured as equivalent width, the inner ring gained about 10 times more than the outer ring lost.
“We don’t know where the extra material is coming from, but there are some hypotheses,” Santos-Sanz said.
The ghost moon
The leading explanation, Santos-Sanz explains, is a small shepherd satellite sharing the outer ring’s orbit. Such an object should explain the rings’ stability and their sharp edges and could also shed debris that replenishes C1R. “This satellite has not been detected yet, if it exists,” Santos-Sanz said.
A computer model based on JWST data also hints at what the two rings are made of. Santos-Sanz, though, makes it clear that this part of the work is unfinished. “Our feeling after this model is that the inner ring should be composed of bigger particles than the outer ring. The outer ring we think is more dusty,” he said. “But this is a work in progress. I can’t say with certainty, well, this is dusty, this is not.”
The best test, the team argues, would be to catch another Chariklo occultation, this time using visible light, which would separate genuine change from a wavelength effect. “We are searching for new occultations,” Santos-Sanz said. Understanding how rings around small bodies evolve over time, he explains, matters, because Chariklo is not the only one to have them.
Rings are now known around another body from the same category as Chariklo, called Chiron, the dwarf planet Haumea, and the trans-Neptunian object Quaoar. Giant-planet rings are already known to shift over months and years; Saturn’s D ring has measurably shrunk, and Neptune’s Adams arcs rearrange themselves. Now small bodies appear to do it as well.
“I think this work is just a piece of the puzzle,” Santos-Sanz said, “but it could be an important clue for broader studies about the rings around minor bodies and around giant planets.”
Jacek Krywko is a freelance science and technology writer who covers space exploration, artificial intelligence research, computer science, and all sorts of engineering wizardry.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : les designers d’Apple dévoilent les secrets de sa conception
articles.text:
Comment concevoir un smartphone pliant qui ne donne pas l'impression d'utiliser deux appareils différents ? Les équipes d'Apple reviennent sur les choix de design, l'interface et les inspirations qui ont guidé la conception de l'iPhone Duo.
Pour concevoir l’iPhone Duo, Apple a puisé dans ce qu’elle avait déjà appris avec l’iPhone, l’iPad et le Mac. Dans un entretien accordé au magazine GQ, John Ternus, Molly Anderson et Steve Lemay reviennent sur le travail mené autour de ce premier modèle pliant. Leur objectif : proposer davantage de surface d'affichage tout en conservant un appareil compact et facile à transporter. La marque à la pomme a aussi cherché à rendre le passage d'un écran à l'autre le plus naturel possible, jusque dans la forme du téléphone, la charnière et l'interface.
iPhone Duo : un format inspiré des carnets de notes et du papier
Pour imaginer un smartphone à la fois spacieux et suffisamment compact pour être transporté facilement, Molly Anderson, vice-présidente du design industriel chez Apple, est partie d'un objet on ne peut plus familier : le carnet de notes. Une référence qui a permis aux designers d'Apple de réfléchir à une question simple : comment gagner en surface d'affichage sans transformer le téléphone en appareil encombrant une fois rangé dans une poche ?
Cette inspiration se retrouve jusque dans la forme de l'iPhone Duo. Pour ses proportions, la firme américaine s'est inspirée des formats de papier A4, A5 et autres déclinaisons de la série A. L'iPhone Duo conserve ainsi le même rapport entre ses dimensions, qu'il soit plié ou déplié.
La charnière a elle aussi fait l'objet d'un travail minutieux de la part des ingénieurs de la pomme : celle-ci doit s'ouvrir facilement, puis maintenir fermement l'iPhone Duo lorsqu'il est complètement déplié. Un choix de conception sur lequel Molly Anderson est revenue dans l'entretien accordé à GQ.
Apple veut éviter l'impression de deux appareils réunis
Côté logiciel, Steve Lemay, vice-président du design de l’interface utilisateur chez Apple, explique que l’objectif était simple : une fois déplié, l’iPhone Duo doit donner l’impression d’être toujours le même appareil, avec davantage d’espace à l’écran. Il affirme qu'il était primordial pour les équipes que l'iPhone Duo « ressemble dès le départ à une expérience cohérente, et non à deux produits différents maladroitement assemblés ». Autrement dit, déplier le téléphone doit donner l'impression d'agrandir naturellement l'appareil que l'on a déjà en main.
Pour y parvenir, Apple a conservé la position et l'apparence des commandes entre les deux configurations du téléphone. Une fois l'iPhone Duo déplié, l'utilisateur retrouve ainsi immédiatement ses repères. Même l'animation de transition aperçue lors de la keynote ne relève pas uniquement de l'esthétique : elle a été pensée pour donner l'impression que l'écran intérieur se déploie naturellement sous l'écran extérieur.
Lemay cite notamment le Mac parmi les principales sources d'inspiration pour l'interface de l'iPhone Duo, avec l'iPad et les iPhone actuels. Le géant de Cupertino a ainsi cherché à reprendre ce qui fonctionne déjà sur ses différents appareils pour l'adapter au format pliant.
Et pour la suite, le designer compte aussi sur les développeurs d'applications, qui pourront imaginer des façons inédites d’exploiter le format pliant de l’iPhone Duo : « Il y a tellement de choses qu'ils vont imaginer que nous n'avons jamais anticipées. Certaines deviendront de grandes idées qui prendront le dessus dans le secteur et feront évoluer le produit de manière intéressante ».

articles.title: Une première pour le Starship : voilà minute par minute ce que la fusée géante de SpaceX va tenter
articles.text:
Ce sera une journée à marquer d’une pierre blanche pour SpaceX, si tout se passe comme prévu. Le mardi 22 septembre 2026, l’entreprise américaine procédera au quatorzième vol d’essai du Starship. À cette occasion, la fusée géante sera testée sur une trajectoire totalement inédite pour elle : sa mise en orbite autour de la Terre.
Jusqu’ici, le lanceur était cantonné à des trajectoires sous-orbitales, afin de valider un socle technique suffisamment robuste pour pouvoir se projeter dans les étapes d’après. Parmi les objectifs de ces tirs, la mise au point d’un étage supérieur (le Ship) suffisamment tenace pour supporter une rentrée dans l’atmosphère sans se désintégrer ni se crasher.
Les treize premiers vols ont finalement permis à SpaceX d’y arriver, non sans mal. Maintenant, c’est une nouvelle phase du développement qui s’est ouverte, avec l’ambition d’aboutir à un engin pleinement réutilisable, et que l’on peut rapidement remettre en selle. Y compris, donc, du côté du bouclier thermique – une pièce sensible et très exposée.
On connaît déjà les grands paramètres du vol du 22 septembre : il sera de longue durée (environ dix heures), à une altitude inférieure à celle de l’ISS (275 km) et assez véloce pour pouvoir boucler six tours de la Terre (à près de 28 000 km/h en orbite terrestre basse). Le booster Super Heavy, qui est la partie basse du Starship, amerrira dans le golfe du Mexique.
Pour ce qui est du Ship, l’activité sera dense : le vaisseau déploiera pour la deuxième fois la nouvelle génération de satellites Starlink V3 (26 unités) – dont trois seront équipées de caméras dédiées à l’inspection directe du bouclier thermique. Cette fois, ces satellites ont vocation à durer dans le temps, en s’intégrant au réseau Starlink.
Le bouclier thermique fera l’objet de plusieurs expérimentations : nouvelles fixations, tuiles incurvées pour réduire l’échauffement aux jonctions, et réutilisation historique de deux tuiles récupérées sur le vol précédent – il s’agit de tester concrètement la réutilisation de pièces usagées et ainsi en tirer toutes les conséquences pour le développement.
Quant au grand final, il arrivera donc plusieurs heures après le décollage. Le Ship tentera une manœuvre d’allumage de désorbitation avant de filer vers l’océan Pacifique, au large du Chili. S’il ne s’est pas désagrégé avant, ou s’il ne s’est pas pulvérisé au contact de l’eau, ce nouveau tir apportera à SpaceX de précieuses informations pour la suite.

articles.title: The Women Powering India’s Semiconductor Revolution
articles.text:
The Women Powering India’s Semiconductor Revolution
Five senior women executives from Teradyne, Micron, Applied Materials, Renesas, and Tata Electronics shared candid career lessons at a SEMICON India 2026 panel moderated by Shradha Sharma.
At SEMICON India 2026 in New Delhi, five senior women leaders from global chip companies came together on stage to talk about what it actually takes for women leaders in the semiconductor industry to rise to the top. The panel, titled "Women Shaping the Electronics and Semiconductor Industry," was held on 18 September 2026, the second day of the three-day event, and was moderated by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project.
The panellists were Alpa Sood, Country Manager at Teradyne India, Usha Gogineni, Director of Technology Development at Micron, Radhika Viswanathan, Chief Operating Officer at Applied Materials India, Malini Narayanamoorthi, President of Renesas India and Vice President at Renesas Electronics, and Lavanya S, Senior Department Manager at Tata Electronics.
SEMICON India 2026 is being held from 17 to 19 September 2026 in New Delhi, jointly organised by the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) and SEMI, and brings together global chipmakers, policymakers, and industry leaders over three days.
Opening the session, Shradha credited Amitesh Kumar Sinha, CEO of the India Semiconductor Mission, for making a deliberate choice to put a panel of women on the SEMICON India stage, noting that earlier editions of the conference had been filled with men. When people talk about R&D and deep tech, men come to mind, she said, admitting that she does it too. She asked the audience to read up on the panellists' accomplishments and go home and tell their stories to their daughters, sisters, and friends.
Five routes into the industry, and one common thread
Alpa, who trained as a lawyer and now leads Teradyne's India business, summed up her role in a line: the engineers make the best products, and she makes sure they reach the people who need them. The job takes resilience first, she said, and it is fine to cry it out as long as you show up the next day with a smile.
Usha described a winding route from IBM in the United States, through a PhD at MIT, to a return to India and a leadership role she had never planned for. She put it down to curiosity, a willingness to try different things, and the adaptability each new thing demanded. Not having a fixed 20-year goal, she said, meant she could take opportunities as they came without seeing them as distractions.
Radhika, who spent a decade on global semiconductor operations strategy and worked on the first project approved under ISM 1.0, recalled a photograph from SEMICON India 2024 showing about 28 men and no women. She kept it on her phone, showed it to her leadership team, and said it was part of why she moved to India in April 2025.
Malini, a mother of two, built her career in applications engineering, chose breadth over depth, and returned to India about five years ago to build and scale Renesas' design team.
Lavanya, who worked at TSMC in Taiwan before joining Tata Electronics to help bring up India's first fab, said TSMC's then chief executive used to say every CEO starts as an engineer. The way forward, regardless of gender, is to take on the hardest projects early.
How they answered the labels women leaders still get
The most pointed exchange came when Shradha asked about a pattern she said holds true globally: women in leadership are labelled either as too emotional or, if demanding, as difficult in ways rarely applied to male bosses with the same standards.
Malini said she was once told she was not ready for a role because she had teared up over something at work, which made her emotional in the eyes of the man assessing her. Her response was to hear him out and then examine honestly whether the criticism was fair, rather than dismiss it or accept it outright. Her conclusion was that she would lead by being genuine, logical, and communicative, and if that came with a tear now and then, it was part of who she was, and the people around her would have to be fine with it.
Alpa's story went back to her first four years at work, when she was repeatedly told a woman should go home early and the more interesting assignments went to others. The one person who backed her was the security guard at her office, where she was among the handful of people who stayed on until midnight. He was not even on duty at that hour, but waited every night until she finished and walked her to her auto-rickshaw. The lesson she took from it was that concern for a woman's safety is real but is not a reason to send her home, that there is always a way to work around it, and that support can come from someone with no obvious stake in your career.
Usha said her early confusion was about what kind of leader to be. Most leaders she had seen were men, and the stereotype was that leaders had to be strict and strong while women were expected to be gentle and empathetic. The one exception in her career, when her first-, second-, and third-line managers at IBM were all women with MIT PhDs, Lisa Su, now CEO of AMD, among them, only underlined how rare that was. Her answer, eventually, was to stop choosing between the two moulds and be authentic, and she said global leaders now recognise that the best style combines both.
Radhika raised a subtler problem: women often get less feedback than men because male managers worry they will take it personally, a point she said Indra Nooyi's autobiography makes well. She credited an Israeli mentor with the line that reframed how she handled pressure, that it is not personal, only business.
Lavanya said that if someone leaves a team saying they do not want to work for a woman, the response is not to take it personally. She urged first-time managers to seek mentors across functions and even at other companies.
Why Are There Still So Few Women In Senior Semiconductor Roles
The numbers explain why this conversation still needs to happen. According to a 2025 report by talent solutions firm NLB Services, women make up about a quarter of India's roughly 220,000-strong chip design and engineering workforce, a share projected to cross 30% by 2027 and reach 35% by 2030. The gap widens sharply at the top, with the same report finding that men hold between 93% and 95% of leadership positions in India's semiconductor sector, leaving women with only 5% to 7% of senior roles.
Part of this comes down to a pipeline that has historically steered fewer women into core engineering and deep-tech specialisations, combined with what Malini called the many points at which a career can "slide off": marriage, childbirth, a child's schooling. Her advice was that these are not exits if you are creative about balancing them and keep going.
Asked what practical advice they would give a teenager, the panellists were specific.
Lavanya said girls are still routinely steered toward information technology for their BTech and should instead take up electronics and communication or electrical engineering, backed by internships that put them on bigger projects. Usha told young women not to be limited by their gender or to software alone, and said women tend to overthink the difficulties they will face when, in her experience, the challenges are minor and credibility earns recognition.
Alpa's advice was to learn business and finances early and to build situational intelligence, the knack of reading a room and working out how to move things. Radhika said Sinha had asked her how the industry could stop women quitting early in their careers, and her answer was that the next two decades in semiconductors are likely to offer one of the most rewarding careers available, and that every problem, personal or professional, can be worked through with patience.
As India's semiconductor investments move from announcements toward operating fabs, packaging lines, and design centres, the industry will need a far wider talent pool than it has today. The panellists suggested that closing the leadership gap will depend less on one-off panels and more on whether companies keep building mentorship networks, flexible career paths, and visible role models. Shradha closed by saying the industry is still not telling women's stories properly, and credited ISM for moving from policy to execution in four years and for setting a benchmark by putting these leaders on the SEMICON India stage.
