articles.title: La serie que tienes que ver si te gustan ‘El Padrino’ y ‘Los Soprano’: es buenísima y solo tiene 2 temporadas
articles.text:
Si te gustan El Padrino, Los Soprano, Peaky Blinders y, en general, las películas o series sobre la mafia, esto te interesa. Todas esas producciones tienen un elemento en común: sus protagonistas son una familia de mafiosos capaces de cualquier cosa con tal de seguir creciendo en su jerarquía de poder. Conflictos internos, guerras abiertas con otras familias... La ambición es el motor que los mueve.
Y todo eso es precisamente lo que tiene la serie de la que venimos a hablar hoy. Se trata de MobLand: Tierra de mafiosos. Una producción que se estrenó el año pasado y que enamoró a todos aquellos que la vieron. En Rotten Tomatoes tiene un 88% de valoración, y en Filmaffinity un 7,7, lo que la sitúa como la segunda mejor serie de 2025 solo por detrás de The Pitt. Sin embargo, por un motivo u otro, ha hecho mucho menos ruido del que merecería.
En Mobland: Tierra de mafiosos, el poder está en juego. La serie nos lleva hasta el Londres actual, donde dos familias mafiosas rivales, los Harrigans y los Stevensons, se enfrentan en una batalla que amenaza con derrumbar imperios y arruinar vidas. En medio del fuego cruzado se encuentra Harry Da Souza, un «arreglador», un hombre a las órdenes de la familia Harrigan, con astucia callejera y que sabe muy bien de qué lado están las lealtades cuando chocan fuerzas opuestas.
3 razones para ver MobLand: Tierra de mafiosos
Si la trama general de la serie no te ha parecido suficiente, hay motivos de sobra para ver MobLand: Tierra de mafiosos. El primero es su descomunal reparto. La serie está liderada por Tom Hardy, Pierce Brosnan y Helen Mirren. Es decir, tres de los actores más cotizados de todo Hollywood. Que cualquiera de ellos protagonice un proyecto ya es suficiente para tenerlo en cuenta y ponerlo en la lista de pendientes. Que los tres unan fuerzas hace verla que se convierta en obligación.
Otro motivo para verla es que, a diferencia de muchas series y películas sobre mafiosos, esta se ambienta en el presente. Evidentemente, asentarse en algún periodo histórico anterior siempre otorga un atractivo especial a este tipo de dramas. Pero situarse en la actualidad le otorga un valor más terrenal e incluso realista. Por eso, ver la Gran Bretaña del siglo XXI convertida en el campo de batalla de las mafias es una delicia para cualquier fan del género.
El tercer motivo para ver MobLand: Tierra de mafiosos es que es muy corta. De hecho, su segunda temporada apenas acaba de estrenarse. En ella, a lo largo de diez episodios, los Harrigan intentarán mantener las apariencias ante la amenaza de nuevos rivales que buscan desestabilizar su fracturado imperio criminal.
Por su parte, el astuto y temible 'solucionador' Harry Da Souza estará en la cuerda floja mientras aumentan las tensiones internas en la familia. Cuando la violencia se extiende a todos los aspectos de sus vidas, las lealtades se quiebran, la seguridad es efímera y la lucha por el poder no deja espacio para la compasión.
El primer episodio de la temporada 2 de MobLand: Tierra de mafiosos se estrenó el 18 de septiembre en Paramount+, pero en España estará disponible en exclusiva en SkyShowtime a partir del 21 de septiembre, con un nuevo episodio cada semana.

articles.title: Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: great headphones, but they're really quite expensive (in a crowded market)
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) sound great and feel comfortable to wear, but there are a few rough edges which you wouldn't expect from cans of this price. Still, the sound alone speaks for how great they are.
Pros
- +Very comfortable to wear
- +Impressive, energetic sound
- +Spatial audio works wonders
Cons
- -Design feels surprisingly cheap
- -Poor battery life
- -Tempting to wait for a discount before buying
Why you can trust TechRadar
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen): Two-minute review
Bose often seems to pay more attention to its Ultra-suffix devices, which absolutely make up some of the best noise-cancelling headphones we've tested. And that is perhaps why the second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones — that is to say, those launched in the post-QC 35 II era — took three years to come to market, following the launch of the older QC Headphones in 2023.
These are basically the QuietComfort Ultra Headphones Gen 2 for people who don’t want to pay an arm and a leg for their sound, and given how I only ever see the non-Ultra cans when I’m out and about in the UK (a fact my editor also confirms), I’d wager that this new release is the model people have been waiting for.
Meet the QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen), so named because they’re quiet, thanks to Bose’s sought-after Active Noise Cancellation, and comfortable (thanks to the use of soft protein leather for pads and bands).
Having used them for several weeks, I can say that the latter is definitely true: these are incredibly easy to use for hours on end, without your ears aching or the top of your head feeling sore. You can basically use them until the battery runs down, although that’s partly because the 24-hour battery life is rather poor in 2026.
I’m not convinced on the ANC sell though. Bose has a reputation for industry-leading noise cancellation, and the Headphones Gen 2 are supposed to match the Ultra Headphones Gen 2 in this department. However, after testing the cans on multiple flights, train rides and around several cities, I’m not fully sold on the claim. They’re great at removing background sound, but not flawless; other brands have caught up, and those similarly-priced competitors surpass them in a few ways.
That’s not to say ANC is an actual problem with the QC Headphones Gen 2, but there are several departments which will raise eyebrows. The cans feel quite cheap, rattling in the hand and offering some odd gaps in the body which shouldn’t be there. They’re also quite light in the feature department, more so than you’d expect for the price.
So why have I given the Bose a four-star review? Well, despite a seemingly-unchanged driver set-up from the older models, and an EQ which barely offers you any control over your music, these cans sound fantastic. They offer detailed and precise treble and energetic and punchy bass. Because of this, listening to tune after tune on them never gets old. The spatial audio is great too, adding an immersive slant to the already-great sound.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Despite quirks, I really enjoyed using the Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2; you will too if you can find them for a price that makes sense. I’m not sure they justify the premium price tag right now, but if you find them discounted, they’re a must-buy.
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Price and release date
- Launched in August 2026
- Sells for $359 / £299 / AU$549.99
- Comes with carry case and two cables
The Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) were announced on August 6, 2026. That’s three years after the first-gen model came out, and a year after the Ultra Gen 2.
Despite not being the ‘Ultra’ member of the family, the ‘standard’ QuietComforts aren’t cheap. You can pick up the cans for $359 / £299 / AU$549.99, which is cheaper in the UK but more expensive in the US than the last-gen models (and the same cost in Australia). It is, of course, cheaper than the Ultra Gen 2 model, which launched for $449 / £449 / AU$699 and haven’t seen a massive price cut since.
So they’re premium headphones, if not ultra-premium ones. They undercut the likes of the Bowers & Wilkins PX7 S3 and Sony WH-1000XM6 (though the newer WH-1000XM4C are cheaper in most regions).
You can pick the cans up in five color options: black, white, mauve, mint and green you see depicted. In the box you get a protective carry case, USB-C to USB-C wire and a USB-C to 3.5mm cable.
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Specs
| Drivers | Not specified | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | 
| Battery life | 24 | 
| Weight | 241g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.4, USB-C | 
| Frequency response | Not specified | 
| Waterproofing | None | 
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Features
- ANC great, but not best
- Poor 24h battery life
- App doesn't offer that much
At 24 hours, the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) don’t have a very long battery life. I’ve tested other options this year which last for literally 100 extra hours; don’t buy these if you need something for a long-haul flight. That listening time is with ANC turned on; you’ll get a few hours more if you turn it off, but less if you use some of the other listening features.
You charge the cans via their USB-C port, which takes 3 hours according to Bose. A new feature for the Gen 2 model is that you can also enjoy wired audio from this port, which is a real get for people who like high-quality audio. It almost makes up for the lack of a 3.5mm jack!
I suppose we should discuss that ANC. As mentioned in the introduction, it was good but not great, and certainly not the best I’ve ever used in over-ear headphones. The difference was small but noticeable: on a flight, I could hear the hum of the engines more than in some other cans I’ve tested, and surrounding sounds would creep into my music more often than I’d like.
They’re not bad by any means, and they’re still some of the better ANC headphones I’ve tested. But they’re not the best, and that’s a surprise given the name and the price point.
The headphones offer a range of listening modes beyond ‘standard’ ANC (which it calls Quiet mode), but I was surprised by how much most of these also affected audio quality. I’d recommend only sticking to Quiet or Aware, which lets in some surrounding sound.
You can toggle between these modes in Bose’s app, which has a few other tools. You can set up multi-point connection, change what that shortcut button does, check the battery life, set up immersive audio and play with the equalizer.
If your ears perked up at the mention of EQ, don’t get too excited. The custom mode only offers 3-band control, and there are four presets which change these three bands for bass or treble reduction or boost. It’s a surprisingly lightweight amount of customization for premium headphones, and people who like to tweak their audio sound will be greatly disappointed.
To be honest, that’s my general takeaway from the Bose app: it offers only a fraction of the tools, features and customization that you’d get from cans costing a third of the price.
One stand-out is Immersive Audio though. In the past, I've found similar offerings from rival brands a tad gimmicky, but Bose’s works very well. You can choose between Still or Motion (depending if you’re still or in motion), and it’ll deliver an encompassing sound that spreads the sound of your music or movie around you. It’s not so overt as to be distracting, and makes music a little more immersive — though I much preferred Still mode, which had a more audible spread which changed as I moved my head.
- Features score: 3/5
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Design
- Comfortable to wear for long periods
- Smartly-placed and designed buttons
- A few cheap-feeling elements
The second-gen Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) look pretty similar to the original pair, but with some refinements in the looks department. Hinges and the retractable arm are better hidden, and the headband’s padding looks better integrated. The cans make the older model look like a prototype.
Oddly, though, the headphones feel pretty cheap. The cups rattle, there’s a noticeable seam between the headband and pad, and parts of the headphones flop around unsupported when you hold the gadget by its headband. There are a few other similar traits which make the buds feel loose, most noticeably that there’s a worrying amount of flex in the band. After several weeks of testing, I’ve yet to have these traits manifest in any actual problem, but I’m constantly surprised by how the build quality flags behind half-priced rivals.
I do appreciate that they're based on a design many users have loved, for many years — and this is likely the key reason they've largely been kept as-is (or was). But still, in the intervening years competing design teams have worked hard on other, newer headphones, and the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) feel a little flimsy and clunky in direct comparison today.
At least the QuietComfort are supremely comfortable to wear. The padding which rests across the top of your head, and the soft cups, both go a long way in ensuring you can listen for long periods of time without getting any aches or strains. It gives the impression of them being light, even though at 241g, they weigh about the same as many other pairs.
When you’re wearing the cans, the right cup has the volume and pause/play buttons; their prominence is different so you can easily tell what button your finger is on. The right edge has the shortcut button, and power slider; I love this latter, as it’s easy to flick to instantly turn the cans on, without needing to press and hold like you do on most rivals. Bose has really nailed the buttons here, which I admit is a small detail, but that is where the devil is according to the idiom.
There’s a decent amount of malleability here: you can rotate the cups a fair way left and right, and the band is quite extendable (though it’s fairly stiff, so you’ll have to give it a hearty tug). The cups don’t move much up and down, but they still fit my head well.
You can fold down the QCs to make them more portable, or put them in the travel case. My aforementioned issues with the ‘loose’ feel of the cans returns here; you can’t stack them on a flat surface without them falling over.
- Design score: 4/5
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Sound quality
- V-shaped audio with energetic bass, treble
- Spatial audio sounds great
- Unspecified drivers inside
If you’ve read the design and features sections of this review, you’ll know I’ve had compliments and criticisms in each department. Not so for audio quality.
Bose hasn’t detailed the driver in the QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen), but the previous-gen model had a 40mm unit, and the brand hasn’t boasted any audio improvements beyond generations. It doesn’t need to; the previous models sounded fantastic and the new ones do too.
Out of the box, you’re getting V-shaped sound from the QuietComfort Headphones. Treble is crisp, sharp and detailed, letting you hear tremolo and tones that many other cans miss. Bass is hefty and punchy, but with a precision and control which avoids lower frequencies drowning out the rest of your song.
As is generally the case with headphones offering V-profile audio, the mids lack just a little bit. I’d often notice guitars playing harmonies, piano accompaniments or high alto/low tenor backing vocals that’d be missing the ‘oomph’ I’d like them to have. But you’re not buying the Bose for a neutral sound: this is for fun and energetic music.
The sound set-up of the QuietComforts is best shown in songs like Fitz and the Tantrum’s Man on the Moon, which has hard-hitting vocals and bass but loses its rhythm guitar and strings a little, or The Hoosiers' Automatic Glow, which sees its harmonic synth line dropped to the back of the mix, in favor of the energetic sung word, and rising hook.
To return to the Bose app, you can use the EQ to try and add some emphasis on mids, but I found this only a limited solution which didn’t have much of an effect on the music.
- Sound quality: 5/5
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Value
- Should be top-value earbuds
- Unfortunately, longevity isn't guaranteed
If your headphone equation is simply “I’ll spend more money for better audio”, the Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2 will be a good option. They sound great and they’re comfortable, so you can enjoy music for a long time (at a fairly high cost).
But to me, a few aspects of these headphones make the premium price seem a little too high. The loose-feeling build quality, lack of app features and poor battery life all point to the cost being higher than it should be. If you see the Bose discounted by about $100 / £100 / AU$200, then these will be good-value cans. Alternatively, the previous-gen models should be enjoying a decent price cut due to being a bit older.
As it stands, the Gen 2 are still good buys, but I’d personally save money and buy cheaper headphones. Which in particular? Well, thankfully there's a competition section below…
- Value: 3.5/5
Should I buy the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen)?
| Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | The noise cancellation is great, but the lack of other tools and poor battery life let the Bose down. | 3/5 | 
| Design | The QuietComfort is certainly comfortable, with some smart elements but a cheap-feeling design. | 4/5 | 
| Sound quality | Most people will find these perfect for music. | 5/5 | 
| Value | They're great, but you'd be right to expect a little more for the price. | 3.5/5 | 
Buy them if…
You find other headphones uncomfortable
Many people struggle with headphones because they don't want their head in a musical vice. Try the QCs, they're your best bet.
You want great noise cancellation
It may not be the best in the biz, but it's still very good: if you need solid ANC, you won't be disappointed.
You love immersive audio features
Always listen to your music with spatial enabled? You'll really like how Bose handles the function.
Don’t buy them if…
You need something long-lasting
Many people will find the 24-hour battery life insufficient. Luckily, it's one of the shortest figures I've seen on earbuds; you can do better.
You like tweaking your audio profile
The QC Headphones' equalizer doesn't offer you much control over your music, nor any kind of listening test.
Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) review: Also consider
Looking for alternative over-ears? Here are a few we've tested and would recommend.
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) | Soundcore Space 2 | Sony WH-1000XM6 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Drivers | Not specified | 40mm | 30mm | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Battery life (ANC on) | 24 hours | 50 hours | 30 hours | 
| Weight | 241g | 264g | 254g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.4, USB-C | Unspecified Bluetooth, 3.5mm | Bluetooth 5.3, 3.5mm | 
| Waterproofing | Not specified | Not specified | IPX4 | 
Soundcore Space 2
This affordable pair of cans costs half the amount of the QC Headphones, and its comfort and ANC match Bose. The audio quality isn't quite on par, however, and nor is the spatial audio.
Read our full Soundcore Space 2 review
Sony WH-1000XM6
Bose's closest rival is from Sony; this set costs a little more and also offers fantastic noise cancellation, an incredible sound and useful button controls.
Read our full Sony WH-1000XM6 review
How I tested the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen)
- Tested for roughly four weeks
- Paired with Android phone for Bluetooth, Android tablet for audio
- Used on walks around neighborhood, at work, on flights and on trains
To write this full review, I used the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) for just over four weeks, which gave me time to fully put them through their paces.
For the majority of the testing time, the buds were paired with my Fairphone 6 Plus smartphone, though I plugged them into a Xiaomi tablet using the cable for some wired audio. Over the course of the review I tested them on multiple flights, countless train and bus journeys, while working at home and on various walks around my city.
I listened on Spotify, to my own digital library, for movies on Now TV and videos on YouTube, and various games.
I've been testing gadgets for TechRadar since early 2019, and in that time have used countless pairs of over-ears.
- First reviewed in September 2026
Tom Bedford is a freelance contributor covering tech, entertainment and gaming. Beyond TechRadar, he has bylines on sites including GamesRadar, Digital Trends, Android Police, TechAdvisor, WhattoWatch and BGR. From 2019 to 2022 he was on the TechRadar team as the staff writer and then deputy editor for the mobile team.

articles.title: Trump treads further on free speech with new journalist bans
articles.text:
On Friday, the president threatened to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House. It could have just been another one of his Truth Social fever dreams, but it turns out it’s very real. All three publications were turned away from the White House this morning, NPR reports, marking an escalation in the administration’s war on the First Amendment.
Trump treads further on free speech with new journalist bans
The president’s threat against CNN, MS Now, and Politico was real.
Politico tried to get to the bottom of it, asking why now? It reports that “many senior [White House] staff were surprised by the directive” (what’s new?), and that it was done “while chief of staff Susie Wiles was out of town.” Apparently he’s been talked down from this kind of sweeping move before, but Trump has already banned journalists from the White House. In 2025, he barred AP reporters from the White House and Air Force One; the AP sued and is still in litigation over the matter. He also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s credentials in his first term, though CNN won them back in court. Clearly, the administration is not too worried about adverse judicial rulings.
This isn’t just about a few publications in the White House. It’s part of a broader attack on journalism and the First Amendment that has exploded during Trump’s second term. The Department of Defense (now the Department of War, though that change was not authorized by Congress), has also pushed reporters out of the Pentagon. Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Friday that he “fully supports” Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now, and Politico, blithely stating “we are grateful these outlets already chose to self-deport from the Pentagon” and echoing the president’s bullshit about fake news.
And journalism and broadcast organizations have faced repeated attack by Trump’s FCC, which is wielding its immense power against anyone who dares to question the president’s conduct. The president has proved he is willing to use almost any lever at his disposal to curb critical speech of himself and his government, which is the beating heart of the First Amendment.
The newly-banned organizations will surely challenge this measure in court, and unless our constitutional order has completely fallen apart, they’ll likely win. But that doesn’t erase the damage — the distraction, cost, and chaos that this kind of thing will cause.
Here are statements from CNN, MS Now, and Politico on the bans.
CNN:
Early today, CNN journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. CNN’s mission to report on the US government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism. We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.
We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor.
CNN stands fully behind our White House team.
MS Now:
Earlier this morning, MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White House belongs to the American people, and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars.
MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.
We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters, and our newsroom.
We will continue to report on the president, the administration, and the issues that impact the American people.
Politico, statement from Global Editor In Chief Jonathan Greenberger:
A few minutes ago, our colleague Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House to do her job as a POLITICO reporter. Secret Service denied her entry to the complex and confiscated the pass that allows her access to the White House. We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights.

articles.title: AI in Chip Design: From Code Generation to EDA Orchestration (University of Edinburgh)
articles.text:
Home
                        
       			
					
TECHNICAL PAPERS
		
								September 19th, 2026 - 
								By: Technical Paper Link
								
							
						
Researchers at the University of Edinburgh published a technical perspective titled “LLMs in Digital EDA: A perspective on shifting roles from Generation to Orchestration.”
Abstract Excerpt: “In this Perspective, we instead define three hierarchical roles that reveal how capability accumulates: a Generator that produces design artifacts in a single pass, an Agent that refines outputs through iterative tool feedback, and an Orchestrator that coordinates decisions across EDA-stages. Across published systems, this reveals a syntax trap in which models are trained to produce plausible code rather than physically correct hardware, compounded by fragmented tools and loss of design context that obscure how decisions affect later stages. Comparisons across the three roles show that current approaches struggle to scale to industrial designs, motivating a shift towards a standardised, physics-aware orchestrator that connects tools and agents across the EDA flow for more reliable and accessible hardware design.”

articles.title: Notre cerveau refuse de l'admettre et se trompe complètement, mais au loto la grille 1-2-3-4-5-6 n'a rien de spécial
articles.text:
On annonce un mégajackpot de 5 000 000 euros au Loto, le rêve ! Vous vous décidez à jouer. Vous vous arrêtez à votre bureau de tabac et prenez une grille. Quels numéros choisir ? La règle est simple : vous devez cocher 5 numéros sur une grille de 49 numéros, puis 1 numéro chance sur une grille de 10 numéros. Ce qui fait 19 068 840 grilles possibles ! Incapable de vous décider, vous faites un flash, les numéros sont choisis pour vous par un ordinateur. Vous obtenez la grille suivante : 7-13-21-32-45 pour les 5 numéros et 7 pour le numéro chance. Une bonne grille de loto, vous rentrez chez vous avec l’espoir qu’aujourd’hui sera votre dernier jour de travail.
22 heures, le soir même ! Jackpot non remporté, la grille « gagnante » obtenue par les bouliers de la Française des jeux est 1-2-3-4-5 pour les 5 numéros et 6 pour le numéro chance, ce qui fait la grille 1-2-3-4-5-6. Vous vous dites que c’est impossible d’obtenir une telle combinaison, que le tirage était forcément truqué ou qu’il était impossible que l’ordinateur vous génère une telle grille.
Injustice, voire complot ! Pourtant : les deux grilles ont exactement la même probabilité de sortir. Une chose est certaine : sur les 19 068 840 grilles possibles, chacune d’entre elles a la même probabilité de sortir.
Ce qui nous paraît improbable, ce sont surtout les grilles qui semblent appartenir à des motifs trop réguliers pour relever du hasard. Dans une expérience, des chercheurs ont proposé à 26 individus dans un café français de choisir 2 grilles de loto parmi 14 grilles dont notre grille gagnante. Aucun participant n’a choisi 1-2-3-4-5-6, et tous ont même affirmé qu’il était impossible de gagner avec une telle grille.
Bien qu’une telle grille n’ait jamais été tirée au Loto de la Française des jeux, la combinaison 5-6-7-8-9-10 est sortie, le 1er décembre 2020, à la loterie sud-africaine pour un jackpot d’approximativement 6 000 000 euros. Paradoxalement à l’étude précédemment citée, 20 joueurs avaient choisi cette grille et se sont partagés le jackpot, alors que les tirages précédents ne comptaient pas de gagnant ou seulement un.
Ce paradoxe peut s’expliquer par notre culture du jeu et la différence entre la stratégie du « choisir pour gagner » et celle du « miser sur l’impossible ». Dans le café français, le joueur cherche, parmi les grilles proposées, sa perception du vrai hasard. À l’inverse, au loto sud-africain, il existe toujours un petit groupe pour tenter des grilles régulières soit par superstition, soit par défi. C’est le pari du « Et si ça se produisait ? »
Comment expliquer la perception de l’impossibilité d’une telle grille ?
En sciences cognitives, cette impossibilité s’appelle l’heuristique de représentativité. Dans cette étude menée auprès de 472 personnes, 70 % des participants ont rejeté les suites logiques dans de vraies grilles de loto pour des combinaisons se rapprochant de leur perception du hasard. Cette étude montre aussi que, parmi eux, 84 % ont refusé un avantage financier plutôt que d’échanger leur combinaison contre une grille régulière. Cette heuristique est fondée sur notre idée stéréotypée du hasard.
Une grille comme 1-2-3-4-5-6 est souvent associée à une suite logique tout comme 5-10-15-20-25-5, tandis que 3-17-26-45-49-6 nous semble plus aléatoire et donc plus près de notre idée de « hasard ». Cette dernière grille nous semble plus cohérente pour un jeu de hasard comme le loto et pourtant toutes ses grilles ont mathématiquement la même probabilité de sortir.
Le paradoxe du parieur et les biais cognitifs
Ce refus d’accepter le « vrai » hasard au sens des probabilités peut prendre aussi une autre forme : le sophisme du joueur. Pour un joueur, l’heuristique de représentativité juge une grille impossible par sa forme, tandis que le sophisme du joueur nous fait penser que les tirages sont liés entre eux, comme s’ils avaient une mémoire !
Ce phénomène n’est pas propre au jeu de loto. Selon une anecdote, reprise dans de nombreux ouvrages sur les probabilités, le plus célèbre des exemples remonterait au soir du 18 août 1913, au casino de Monte-Carlo, où la roulette serait tombée 26 fois de suite sur la couleur noire, ce qui n’a qu’une chance sur 67 108 864 de se produire. Gagner au loto est 3,5 fois plus probable !
Défiant l’intuition, les joueurs se seraient mis à miser des sommes de plus en plus importantes sur le rouge. Les joueurs étant convaincus que plus la série de noir augmentait, plus la probabilité d’obtenir un rouge au tour suivant augmentait également. Une soirée lucrative pour le casino ! Ce qui nous échappe, c’est qu’un tour de roulette est indépendant des précédents, la roulette n’a pas de mémoire tout comme les bouliers de la Française des jeux. Dans cet exemple, le sophisme du joueur est un biais statistique. Au loto, un joueur évitera de choisir, par exemple, la même grille que la grille gagnante précédente pensant qu’une même grille ne peut pas gagner successivement.
Au loto, la grille 1-2-3-4-5-6 est tout autant aléatoire que la grille 7-31-42-47-49-2, ces deux grilles ont exactement la même probabilité d’être gagnantes. Une chose est claire, notre cerveau n’aime pas les probabilités et nos biais cognitifs continueront à déjouer les mathématiques et le hasard !
Laurent Delisle, Chercheur associé en Mathématiques, ECE Paris

articles.title: BragJack attacks hijack AI browser agents through malicious extensions
articles.text:
Security researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security has disclosed a new attack technique that can hijack the AI assistants built into popular browsers using a single malicious browser extension.
Dubbed BragJack, the proof-of-concept was demonstrated against five Chromium-based browsers or browser assistants: Google Chrome's Gemini Live, Perplexity Comet, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, and Anthropic's Claude in Chrome.
The research earned more than $20,000 in bug bounties from the five vendors, ranging from $600 to $7,000, and produced two CVEs.
The attack requires the malicious extension to already be installed in the victim's browser.
Once it is, the researcher shows the abuse can run without user interaction, letting an extension control an AI browser agent and abuse its existing privileges to access sensitive information or act on the victim's behalf.
Both Google and Microsoft have since resolved the flaws they were assigned.
Abusing trusted browser components
The attacks exploit the way AI assistants are increasingly wired into browsers and handed browser-level capabilities.
In his writeup, Weizman describes these systems as having a "brain" and a "body." The AI model processes instructions and decides what should happen.
A privileged browser component then performs the actions, such as accessing tabs, reading content, taking screenshots, or interacting with websites.
The problem, according to the researcher, is that browser extensions can manipulate web traffic and pages that these privileged components trust.
The same extension was used across all five targets, relying on Chromium's declarativeNetRequest (DNR) functionality. DNR lets extensions modify how network requests are handled, including changing response headers and redirecting resources.
In the Chrome attack, Weizman found that although extensions were blocked from directly touching the privileged chrome://glic component or injecting scripts into Google's Gemini site, DNR rules could still intercept requests made by the embedded Gemini web app.
By weakening security headers and redirecting a JavaScript resource, he executed code inside the Gemini context, communicating directly with Chrome's privileged AI component rather than going through Gemini's normal request flow.
Weizman says the resulting access could read local files, reach web content, take screenshots, and potentially reach the browser's camera and microphone. Chrome assigned the finding CVE-2026-0628 and paid a $7,000 bounty.
From reading data to controlling AI agents
The attacks against agentic browsers such as Perplexity Comet and Opera Neon go further, because their agents can act on websites rather than merely read them.
For Comet, Weizman found the browser's built-in agent extension trusted several Perplexity domains, including a testing domain that did not get the same protections as the primary perplexity.ai site. By removing a redirect to that domain with DNR, he loaded it and injected a content script able to talk to the built-in agent.
The resulting access included browsing history, screenshots, local files, and the ability to send instructions to the agent. Weizman demonstrated forcing the agent to visit Perplexity, summarize the victim's emails, and send the results to another address.
Microsoft Edge presented a different challenge. Microsoft had split its agent into "Think" and "Do" modes to stop it from taking arbitrary instructions and actions at the same time.
Weizman found a race condition that briefly disables the restriction while forcing a prompt, then re-enables the action capability before the agent checks its state. Microsoft assigned CVE-2026-55945 to the race condition.
Similar flaws were demonstrated against Opera Neon and Claude in Chrome, though the latter is itself a browser extension rather than a browser.
Earlier this year, in my work at Manifold Security, I reported a related weakness in Claude for Chrome: the extension ran its built-in AI workflows on synthetic clicks without verifying they came from a real user, and the flagged code was still reproducible eight releases later.
That followed ClaudeBleed, an earlier flaw in the same extension that LayerX disclosed in April, in which Claude for Chrome trusted the claude.ai origin rather than checking which script was actually driving it.
'Prompt Forcing'
Weizman calls the technique used to seize these agents Prompt Forcing.
Unlike conventional prompt injection, where an attacker tries to slip malicious instructions into content an AI is already reading, Prompt Forcing lets the attacker hand the agent an entire prompt and the follow-up instructions. The agent then translates those instructions into legitimate browser actions using its existing privileges.
That matters for endpoint defenses, the researcher argues, because the final action is not carried out by conventional malicious code. Legitimate software is being told to perform the attack.
BragJack points to a growing challenge as browsers and other endpoint apps gain more capable AI agents. A compromised extension that would traditionally see only web content can, in some designs, become a path to software that reads files, browsing data, and acts on websites for the user.
Users should keep browsers fully updated, remove extensions they do not recognize or no longer use, and treat broad "read and change all your data on all websites" permission prompts with caution.
In addition to his writeup, Weizman has published a full technical breakdown covering all five attacks.

articles.title: On a vu les Shokz OpenFit 2 AI : ces écouteurs veulent devenir votre traducteur et prendre vos notes
articles.text:
On a vu les Shokz OpenFit 2 AI : ces écouteurs veulent devenir votre traducteur et prendre vos notes
Nous avons pu découvrir les Shokz OpenFit 2 AI en avant-première à l’IFA 2026. Toujours fidèles au concept d’écouteurs ouverts de la marque, ces nouveaux modèles ajoutent une dimension supplémentaire qui pourrait bien changer leur usage au quotidien.
Présentés pour la première fois hors de Chine à l’IFA 2026, les Shokz OpenFit 2 AI marquent une nouvelle étape pour le spécialiste des écouteurs ouverts. Ils ont non seulement pour particularité de diffuser de la musique tout en laissant l’utilisateur entendre son environnement, mais aussi de se transformer en outil de productivité. Le produit est déjà commercialisé en Chine, mais aucun lancement n’est pour l’heure prévu en Europe.
Les OpenFit 2 AI embarquent le modèle Qwen et se présentent comme une sorte de boîte à outils IA contrôlable depuis les écouteurs. Les trois fonctionnalités mises en avant par Shokz sont l’enregistrement et la transcription, le compte rendu de réunions et la traduction instantanée.
Jusqu'à 8 h d'enregistrement via les écouteurs ou le boîtier
L’enregistrement peut être déclenché depuis l’un des écouteurs, le boîtier ou l’application Shokz. La marque annonce une portée d’enregistrement allant jusqu’à 5 m dans des environnements contrôlés et jusqu’à 8 h d’enregistrement en stéréo. Un double appui permet également de marquer un passage important pour le retrouver plus facilement par la suite.
Si la captation s’effectue principalement à l’aide des quatre microphones intégrés dans les écouteurs, elle peut aussi être réalisée directement via le boîtier, qui intègre lui aussi un microphone. L’utilisateur peut donc enregistrer lorsque les écouteurs ne sont pas portés, voire lorsqu’ils sont rangés dans leur boîtier. L’enregistrement est ensuite transmis des écouteurs au smartphone, puis directement stocké dans le cloud, avant de pouvoir être consulté au sein de l’app Shokz.
Pour la transcription, Shokz revendique 49 langues et dialectes, répartis en 30 catégories de langues et 19 dialectes chinois. Le français figure bien parmi les langues prises en charge. Le système peut également distinguer plusieurs intervenants afin de faciliter la lecture des transcriptions affichées sur le smartphone.
Après une réunion, l’IA peut générer un résumé avec les principaux sujets abordés, les tâches à effectuer, etc. Shokz annonce que 19 modèles de comptes rendus sont proposés, dont certains adaptés à des domaines comme le droit, la finance, l’informatique, la médecine ou encore le journalisme.
Traduction en face-à-face, directement dans les écouteurs
Les OpenFit 2 AI proposent également plusieurs fonctions de traduction : traduction des appels, traduction en face-à-face et traduction de contenus audio ou audiovisuels. Pour la traduction vocale, Shokz annonce actuellement 11 langues, parmi lesquelles le français, l’anglais, l’allemand, le japonais, le coréen, le russe, le portugais, le thaï, l’indonésien et le vietnamien, en plus du chinois. Les propos de notre interlocuteur, qu’il soit au bout du fil ou directement en face de nous, sont énoncés à voix haute via les écouteurs dans une langue définie au préalable.
Le fait que le français soit déjà pris en charge en Chine ne signifie donc pas que le produit soit immédiatement prêt pour l’Europe. Shokz semble plutôt vouloir valider la qualité et la fiabilité de son expérience multilingue avant de procéder au lancement européen. Pour des fonctions comme la transcription ou la traduction en temps réel, la gestion des accents, des conversations à plusieurs, des contextes professionnels et des différentes variantes linguistiques sont effectivement un enjeu important.
Des OpenFit 2+ boostés à l'IA, sans trop passer à la caisse ?
Outre les fonctions IA, les OpenFit 2 AI reprennent à l’identique la fiche technique des OpenFit 2+. Ils embarquent le principe acoustique DualBoost, qui utilise deux transducteurs par oreillette, tandis que les traitements OpenBass 2.0 et DirectPitch 2.0 renforcent les basses et limitent les fuites sonores. Chaque écouteur pèse environ 9,4 g et se positionne autour de l’oreille à l’aide d’un crochet en titane flexible recouvert de silicone. Surtout, ils demeurent placés à environ un demi-centimètre du conduit auditif, sans y pénétrer, afin d’offrir un confort optimal au quotidien.
Côté autonomie, Shokz annonce jusqu’à 11 h sur une charge et 48 h avec le boîtier. Ce dernier peut être rechargé en USB-C ou via un chargeur sans fil Qi.
Selon nos informations, les OpenFit 2 AI sont actuellement vendus 1500 yuans en Chine, soit environ 200 €. Étant donné que les OpenFit 2+ ont été lancés à 199 € en France, il ne serait pas étonnant que leur prix s’élève à au moins 230 €, compte tenu des fonctions IA supplémentaires.

articles.title: Best Way to Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Got a shiny new iPhone 18 Pro and ready to set it up? Great. But before you get excited, there’s one thing standing between you and a smooth start: your WhatsApp chats.
They won’t transfer from Samsung on their own. If you want to transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro without losing years of conversations and photos, you need a plan.
This guide compares three practical methods, from a no-reset desktop tool to Apple’s own app to a simple chat export.
What to Know Before Transferring WhatsApp
Moving WhatsApp from one Android phone to another? Simple, right? Same system, same backup format. Moving it to an iPhone is different. Android and iOS save WhatsApp backups in totally different ways, so the app can’t just copy files across like it normally would.
Apple does offer an official fix through the Move to iOS app. But it only works if you use it before finishing your iPhone’s setup, and both phones need to sit close together on a steady Wi-Fi connection. Already set up your iPhone? Then this route usually means wiping it and starting over, which is a real headache when all you wanted was to transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro without a full reset.
That’s the gap Tenorshare iCareFone WhatsApp Transfer was built to fill.
How to Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro
Don’t know how to transfer WhatsApp from Android to iPhone? You’ve got three options:
- A desktop tool that skips the factory reset.
- Apple’s own free Move to iOS app.
- WhatsApp’s Email Chat feature for saving individual conversations.
Each one solves a different problem. Let’s go through them.
Method 1: Best Way to Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone Without Factory Reset
Best for: Anyone whose iPhone 18 Pro is already set up, or anyone who just doesn’t want to erase and restart their new phone to move chats over.
Tenorshare iCareFone WhatsApp Transfer is a desktop program made for exactly this situation. It’s built to transfer WhatsApp from Android to iPhone even after the iPhone has already been through setup. A few things worth knowing about it:
- Skips the factory reset: You can transfer WhatsApp from Android to iPhone after setup, no erasing required.
- Lets you pick what moves: Choose specific chats, photos, and videos, or merge old and new WhatsApp data instead of overwriting everything.
- Works across brands: Built to handle Samsung and other Android phones moving to any current iPhone, including a fresh WhatsApp transfer from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro setup.
Here’s how it works:
- Download and install iCareFone WhatsApp Transfer on your pc. Then plug in both your Samsung phone and your iPhone 18 Pro with USB cables and click “Transfer.” This is the first step to transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro.
- Follow the steps to back up WhatsApp on your Samsung phone. At some point, you’ll need to scan an end-to-end encryption key.
- When the backup is complete, select the chats and attachments you want to transfer, and make sure WhatsApp is login on your iPhone.
- Click “Restore” and let the program work. Your iPhone 18 Pro will restart once the transfer wraps up.
Method 2: Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone with Move to iOS
Best for: People setting up a brand-new iPhone 18 Pro who haven’t gone through the setup yet.
Move to iOS is Apple’s own free app, and it’s the easiest option if you’re starting fresh. It’ll transfer WhatsApp messages from Android to iPhone for free, plus your contacts, photos, and a bunch of other stuff- all in one shot while you’re setting up the phone.
The one downside: this only works during initial setup. It won’t work when your iPhone is active.
Here’s how it works:
- Grab the Move to iOS app from the Google Play Store on your Samsung.
- Start setting up your iPhone 18 Pro. When you reach “Transfer Your Apps & Data,” tap “From Android.”
- Open Move to iOS on your Samsung phone, click Continue, and accept the terms.
- Type in the code your iPhone shows you, choose what to bring over, including WhatsApp, then just wait it out on both devices.
Method 3: Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone via Email Chat
Best for: Folks who just need to keep a few important texts handy, not the entire chat history. Keep in mind you’ll only end up with a copy of that single conversation to read later, nothing more.
Email Chat sends one conversation as a text file straight to your email, and you can include the photos or videos too if you want. But keep in mind, this isn’t a real transfer. Your chats won’t show up inside WhatsApp on your iPhone. You get a copy of the conversation you can read later.
Here’s how it works:
- Open the WhatsApp chat you want to save on your Samsung.
- Click on the three dots, then “More,” then “Export chat.”
- Choose “Include Media” or “Without Media,” then pick your email app to send it.
- Send the email to yourself, then open it on your iPhone 18 Pro to view or save the file.
Comparison: Which Method Should You Choose to Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone?
Not sure which fits best? The best method depends on your setup, transfer needs, and whether you want a complete migration or only selected chats. The comparison below highlights the key differences so you can choose the option that fits your situation.
| Feature | iCareFone Transfer | Move to iOS | Email Chat | 
| Works after iPhone setup | Yes | No, need reset | Yes | 
| Full chat history moved | Yes | Yes | No, one chat at a time | 
| Factory reset required | No Free | Yes, if already set up | No | 
| Cost | Paid, free preview | Free | Free | 
| Best for | Full migration. No reset | New iPhone setup | Saving a few chats | 
FAQs
- How Can I Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone for Free?
Apple’s Move to iOS app is free. You can move WhatsApp chats during iPhone setup. The catch is timing: it only works before you finish the setup process, so it’s really meant for people activating a brand-new phone.
- Can I Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone Without a Factory Reset?
Yes, but only if you use a desktop tool like iCareFone WhatsApp Transfer. It connects to both phones at once and moves your WhatsApp data over without wiping an iPhone you’ve already set up, something Move to iOS just can’t do.
- Can Smart Switch Transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone?
Nope. Smart Switch only works between Samsung and other Android or Samsung phones; it just doesn’t connect to iOS. So if you’re switching from Samsung to iPhone, you have to use Move to iOS, a third-party transfer tool, or WhatsApp’s own export option.
- Can I Restore a Google Drive WhatsApp Backup on an iPhone?
No, iPhones and Android phones use different backup systems. Transfer of WhatsApp messages from Android to iPhone using Google Drive isn’t possible, as WhatsApp can’t read a Google Drive backup on iOS. Some transfer tools are made to pull data from a Google Drive backup and restore it onto your iPhone.
- Will My WhatsApp Messages, Photos, and Videos Transfer to iPhone 18 Pro?
A dedicated transfer tool or Move to iOS can bring over messages, photos, and videos together. Email Chat handles only one conversation at a time, with media as an optional add-on, so it won’t rebuild your whole chat library on the new phone.
Conclusion
There’s no single best way to transfer WhatsApp from Samsung to iPhone 18 Pro; it depends on your situation. Move to iOS is best for a new setup, while Email Chat is best for keeping a small number of conversations. If your iPhone is already set up or you want to avoid a factory reset, Tenorshare iCareFone WhatsApp Transfer is a practical option to consider for moving your chats and media.

articles.title: Des robots débarquent dans 30 appartements pour faire le ménage : voici le résultat
articles.text:
Ce jeudi 17 septembre 2026, l’entreprise californienne Figure a présenté Helix 2.5, un nouveau modèle IA qui permet au robot humanoïde Figure 03 de percevoir son environnement, comprendre ce qu’il doit faire et contrôler ses mouvements. Figure a par ailleurs entraîné son modèle Helix 2.5 à partir d’Index, sa vaste base de données regroupant des vidéos de comportements humains. Pour montrer les capacités d’Helix 2.5, Figure a décidé de louer 30 appartements dans la baie de San Francisco et d’y lâcher ses robots.
30 logements pour mettre les robots à l’épreuve
Les robots Figure 03 sont arrivés dans des logements qu’ils ne connaissaient pas. Leur objectif a été d’accomplir trois tâches ménagères spécifiques : ranger des pièces, plier des serviettes et faire le lit. Le point le plus important à retenir : ces logements n’avaient jamais été cartographiés par l’entreprise. Les robots ont donc fait face à des environnements totalement inconnus, selon Figure. En revanche, la base de données Index leur a permis d’accomplir ces tâches. En effet, des humains ont effectué sans relâche des tâches ménagères, tout en filmant leurs actions grâce à une caméra placée juste au-dessus de leurs yeux, comme nous pouvons le voir à la quatrième minute de la vidéo ci-dessous. Le modèle Helix 2.5 a ensuite intégré ces vidéos pour permettre aux robots de reproduire les gestes ménagers réalisés par des humains.
Le robot Figure 03 n’a pas dû participer à un concours de tri de colis : ses tâches ont simplement été de ranger des pièces, faire le lit et plier des serviettes. À chaque serviette mal pliée ou à chaque lit mal fait, le robot perdait un point. Son taux de réussite a été de 56 % sur l’ensemble des tests réalisés dans les 30 logements. Un résultat en demi-teinte donc, mais qui annonce tout de même de sérieux progrès dans le domaine.
Brett Adcock, fondateur et PDG de Figure, explique à propos de cette démonstration : « Helix 2.5 a été conçu pour répondre à une question plus complexe : un robot humanoïde peut-il entrer dans une maison qu’il n’a jamais vue et se mettre immédiatement au travail, en utilisant tout son corps, de manière autonome ? ».
C’est tout le challenge de la robotique actuellement : pouvoir placer un robot dans un environnement ou face à un objet totalement inconnu (comme une friteuse) et qu’il parvienne à se débrouiller de façon autonome. Si certains robots parviennent à réaliser des prouesses, la majorité d’entre eux ne parvient pas à nouer les lacets d’une chaussure.
Des robots feront bientôt notre lit ?
L’entreprise Figure reconnaît elle-même que ses robots ne sont pas encore prêts à intégrer des maisons. Cependant, elle estime qu’Helix 2.5 présente « les premiers signes d’une intelligence physique plus générale », soit une IA capable de comprendre le monde réel et d’y agir de façon autonome, via un robot.
Les robots qui font nos lits et rangent le salon n’arriveront donc pas demain la veille, mais ce n’est qu’une question de temps. Tesla prépare activement son robot Optimus, même si sa conception semble très compliquée, et nous n’allons même pas parler de la Chine qui compte commercialiser des robots à bas prix. L’avenir des robots se jouera assurément dans nos salons : il reste à savoir quand.

articles.title: Diese chinesische Solarzelle liefert Strom – aus 10 Metern Meerestiefe
articles.text:
Unterwasser-Solarzellen: Chinesische Forscher erzeugen Strom in 10 Metern Tiefe
China treibt längst Photovoltaik-Projekte in großem Umfang auf dem Meer voran, um für die Energiegewinnung keine teuren Flächen in Küstennähe zu verschwenden. Allein die Provinz Jiangsu an der Ostküste China hat zuletzt ein Offshore-Solarprogramm im Umfang von gut 27 Gigawatt gestartet.
Solarzellen erzeugen unter Wasser Strom
Kombiniert werden die Vorhaben jeweils mit Energiespeichern, wie pv magazine schreibt. Doch in China sollen Solaranlagen offenbar nicht nur auf, sondern künftig auch tief im Meer Energie erzeugen. Entsprechende Solarzellen haben Forscher:innen der chinesischen Yunnan University jetzt entwickelt.
Konkret handelt es sich um Unterwasser-Perowskit-Solarzellen, die genau jene Wellenlängen von Sonnenlicht absorbieren können, die tief ins Meer vordringen. Die Forscher:innen bauten dazu zunächst ein Testsystem, um das Sonnenlicht in verschiedenen Meerestiefen zu simulieren, wie die Futurezone berichtet.
Perowskit-Solarzelle nutzt blaues Licht im Meerwasser
Die mithilfe der aus den Tests erzielten Daten entwickelten die Forscher:innen eine Perowskit-Zelle, die blaues bis orangenes Licht verwerten kann. Die Solarzelle wurde anschließend skaliert. Entstanden ist ein Modul in der Größe, die auch bei kommerziellen Projekten zum Einsatz käme.
Montiert auf einem Unterwasserroboter erzeugte das Modul in zehn Meter Meerestiefe innerhalb von zwei Stunden 324 Milliwattstunden Strom. Weil es sich überhaupt um den ersten Test unter Realbedingungen handelte, zeigten sich die Forscher:innen von dem Ergebnis überrascht. Die Menge an Energie würde nämlich ausreichen, um einen kleinen Lithium-Ionen-Akku zu laden oder ein LED-Licht zu betreiben.
Yunnan University testet Solarmodule in größeren Meerestiefen
Die Forscher:innen wollen in weiteren Tests nicht nur die Stromausbeute erhöhen, sondern auch austesten, bis zu welcher Tiefe Solaranlagen im Meer Energie erzeugen können. Schon jetzt soll feststehen, dass das Modul in zehn Meter tiefem Salzwasser rund 5,5 Jahre Energie liefern könnte.
Die Einsatzmöglichkeiten sind jedenfalls vielfältig. Laut den Forscher:innen könnten damit etwa Tauchroboter mit Strom versorgt werden, die Wartungsarbeiten an Unterwasser-Infrastruktur vornehmen. Auch ließen sich Kommunikationsbojen und Unterwasserkameras sowie Sensoren betreiben.
Unterwasser-Solarzellen versorgen Tauchroboter, Sensoren und Bojen
Denkbar wäre auch die Möglichkeit, Schiffen eine Art Steckdosenboje zur Verfügung zu stellen, damit diese den Einsatz von klimaschädlichen Generatoren minimieren können. Ihre Ergebnisse haben die Forscher:innen in Form einer Studie im Fachmagazin Joule veröffentlicht.

articles.title: En ce mois de rentrée, ce laptop de Lenovo avec son écran OLED de 16" passe sous les 900 euros et un sac à dos est offert — Frandroid
articles.text:
En ce mois de rentrée, Darty pense à ceux qui reprennent le travail et ceux qui retrouvent les bancs de l’école. Ainsi, l’enseigne a mis au point un pack composé du polyvalent Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 et d’un sac à dos. Cet ensemble est à retrouver pour moins de 900 euros grâce à une remise de presque 20 %.
Les atouts de ce pack Lenovo :
- Un écran OLED de 16 pouces
- L’Intel Core Ultra 5, 16 Go de RAM et 512 Go de stockage
- Un sac à dos pour le transport
Ce pack est habituellement proposé pour 1 099,99 euros, mais chez Darty, il chute à 899,99 euros.
L’IdeaPad Slim 5 tape dans l’œil
En sortant ce Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 de son carton, vous n’allez pas être surpris par son design puisqu’il reste dans la norme des ultrabooks. Il est fin avec 1,7 cm d’épaisseur pour un poids de 1,75 kg tandis que son coloris gris est passe-partout. La connectique est aussi complète avec deux ports USB-A, deux ports USB-C, un port HDMI, un espace pour une carte microSD et un combo jack.
Néanmoins, ce Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 surprend lorsque vous allez l’ouvrir. D’abord, le pavé numérique n’est pas situé au centre, mais il est décalé sur la gauche. Ensuite, la bordure supérieure n’est pas uniforme et présente une légère encoche qui héberge la webcam.
Une fois allumé, le PC portable de Lenovo offre une belle image grâce à sa dalle OLED de 16 pouces affichant une résolution de 1 920 x 1 200 pixels. Cependant, cet écran n’est pas parfait puisque sa luminosité plafonne à 300 nits, ce qui n’est pas idéal pour une utilisation en extérieur.
Un PC portable présent sur tous les fronts
Les surprises se poursuivent pendant l’utilisation de ce PC portable puisque, malgré sa finesse, il est assez polyvalent. Lenovo l’a doté d’un Intel Core Ultra 5 et de 16 Go de RAM. Une configuration qui permet d’effectuer des tâches bureautiques et créatives, tout en ayant plusieurs onglets ouverts sans que l’ordinateur ne ralentisse.
Si vous souhaitez monter des vidéos, cet IdeaPad Slim 5 peut montrer quelques limites sur les projets les plus demandeurs en ressources, notamment ceux qui incluent des éléments en 3D.
Enfin, ce PC portable s’accompagne d’un sac à dos, lui aussi estampillé Lenovo. Celui-ci se compose d’une grande poche. À l’intérieur, on retrouve un espace dédié au rangement de l’ordinateur.
Avec cette promotion de Darty, ce Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 rejoint la catégorie des PC portables à moins de 1 000 euros. Pour découvrir les meilleurs produits situés dans cette tranche tarifaire, rendez-vous dans ce guide.

articles.title: En algunos pueblos de China un médico atiende a más de 2.000 personas. La IA empieza a convertirse en su segunda opinión
articles.text:
Me considero una afortunada: si pido cita para mi médica en mi pueblo, en menos de 48 horas suelo poder acudir a resolver cualquier dolencia. Sé que si la cita es con un especialista la cosa cambia y que en otras localizaciones dentro del estado, la espera se dilata. Poco personal y muchos pacientes es la receta para el desastre sanitario.
Eso pasa aquí y también en China, donde China Daily recoge el caso de Zhang Qifang, médico de 68 años que atiende el solito a 2.000 personas en Pu'an, en la provincia de Guizhou. Y ojo porque no es algo nuevo: el galeno explica que lleva tres décadas con esa cartera de pacientes milenaria en la China rural. Así que a falta de personal, ha acogido con los brazos abiertos el proyecto Ant Afu, que aplica la IA a la medicina.
Qué hace la IA en concreto. Ya sabíamos que la inteligencia artificial puede sacar notazas en exámenes de medicina, pero una cosa es el papel y otra los pacientes, lo que te dicen, lo que no y cómo te lo dicen. Y ahí la historia cambia. Por eso Ant Afu, matriz de Alipay, no ha convertido la IA en un médico para hablar con los pacientes sino en un asistente para facultativos.
Da acceso a una base de conocimiento médico amplia, ayuda a los profesionales de la medicina a orientar diagnósticos o permite analizar un informe o una analítica donde los humanos tienen dudas y necesitan un apoyo. Además, esta aplicación se orienta donde más se necesita: en la sanidad rural, donde más se necesita.
Por qué importa. Más allá de las vivencias del galeno Zhang Qifang, hay un problema estructural que China está atajando con IA. Así, la inteligencia artificial llega al rescate donde faltan especialistas de forma crónica, algo que le pasa al país asiático pero no es exclusivo de allí: pasa en la España profunda, en la India o en zonas rurales de Latinoamerica. En pocas palabras: es un proyecto que puede replicarse.
En una época en la que la tecnología está creando brechas digitales (esa odisea de mi madre para pedir citas previas), este es un ejemplo de justo lo contrario: es un caso de tecnología inclusiva. Hay quien ve a la IA como un motor para potenciar la productividad, pero en este caso es más bien una herramienta para reducir las desigualdades sanitarias y mejorar la atención.
La (otra) vieja y rural China. Puede que China viva en el futuro, tenga trenes bala o drones y que sea la fábrica del mundo, pero una cosa son las grandes y tecnológicas ciudades como Shenzhen, Shanghai o Pekín y otra el campo. Como explica el medio chino, el país asiático sufre un gran desequilibrio entre la ciudad y el campo que va más allá de distancias y personal: es un problema estructural.
En lo rural, sus pacientes son mayoritariamente ancianos que sufren enfermedades crónicas y además, algunos médicos rurales adolecen de formación especializada que sí tienen sus colegas urbanitas. De hecho, el propio Zhang cuenta un caso de hipertiroidismo en 1999 que no supo diagnosticar. En pocas palabras, en el campo hay menos médicos, están menos actualizados y también están envejecidos... como buena parte de sus pacientes.
Bajo el capó. Ant Afu no es como decirle a Gemini o a ChatGPT que te duele la cabeza (algo que quien más quien menos ha hecho de vez en cuando): funciona con un modelo de IA médico propio de Ant Group llamado Ant Medical que la empresa liberó como código abierto a principios de este año. De hecho, es uno de los modelos médicos abiertos más grandes que existen, con 100.000 millones de parámetros y para su entrenamiento se usó datos clínicos reales y se ajustó para razonar como un médico.
Como curiosidad, ha quedado primer en varios benchmarks de IA aplicados a la medicina como HealthBench, de OpenAI. No obstante y como nadie es infalible, si la IA no es suficiente, puede conectarse a una red de 300.000 doctores.
Las cifras del despliegue. Desde febrero de 2026, 170 médicos rurales del área de Pu'an han recibido formación en el uso de esta IA y desde junio el proyecto se ha extendido geográficamente a Meizhou (Guangdong), de modo que ya está disponible para dos de cada tres médicos locales. En estos momentos, Ant Afu ya opera en 4 provincias y 27 prefecturas o ciudades, dando servicio combinado a 70.000 médicos rurales y de familia en toda China.
Es solo el principio. La información procede de la puesta de largo del proyecto en el Inclusion Conference de Shanghai, un evento donde la empresa responsable y principal interesada cuenta sus ventajas por lo que, aunque el despliegue sea relativamente grande, todavía está en fases iniciales: es pronto para conocer su precisión diagnóstica real, su tasa de error o su impacto.

articles.title: Inversores cuestionan si Anthropic podrá sostener sus ingresos después de salir a bolsa
articles.text:
Anthropic afronta dudas entre potenciales inversores sobre su capacidad para mantener el extraordinario crecimiento de sus ingresos una vez que salga a bolsa. La compañía, creadora del chatbot Claude, alcanzó unos ingresos anualizados de 65.000 millones de dólares en julio y sus inversores prevén que supere los 120.000 millones de dólares al cierre de 2026.
El problema no está en el crecimiento actual, sino en cuánto tiempo puede mantenerse. La competencia de OpenAI y de modelos de IA más baratos, la sensibilidad de los clientes a los precios, la concentración de los ingresos y los elevados costes asociados al desarrollo de sistemas avanzados están entre los factores que generan incertidumbre antes de una posible oferta pública inicial (OPV).
PUBLICIDAD
Anthropic está valorada actualmente en unos 965.000 millones de dólares. Personas familiarizadas con el desempeño de la compañía citadas por Financial Times sitúan las posibles valoraciones tras la salida a bolsa entre 1,5 y 4 billones de dólares, una diferencia que refleja las dudas sobre el ritmo de crecimiento futuro.
OpenAI vuelve a presionar a Anthropic
Uno de los principales desafíos procede de OpenAI. Según datos de OpenRouter, el lanzamiento de GPT-5.6 en julio permitió a la compañía recuperar cuota de gasto de los usuarios y superar a Anthropic en gasto semanal por primera vez en más de dos años y medio.
La competencia no se limita a las dos empresas estadounidenses. Los llamados modelos de código abierto, cuyos parámetros pueden estar disponibles públicamente y que pueden ser modificados por empresas y desarrolladores, también están ganando terreno.
PUBLICIDAD
Compañías como DeepSeek y Moonshot, además de Meta, están desarrollando modelos que se acercan al rendimiento de algunos sistemas cerrados de última generación. Al tener costes potencialmente menores y permitir una mayor personalización, estas alternativas pueden facilitar que las empresas cambien de proveedor.
Eric Glyman, cofundador y codirector ejecutivo de la compañía de pagos Ramp, explicó al Financial Times que por primera vez está observando una competencia significativa en precios entre los laboratorios de IA. Ramp, añadió, ha reducido un 40 % su gasto en inteligencia artificial y utiliza diferentes modelos dependiendo de la tarea.
La fidelidad de los usuarios es otro factor
La presión sobre los precios plantea una cuestión fundamental para Anthropic: si sus clientes seguirán pagando por sus modelos cuando existan alternativas capaces de ofrecer resultados similares por menos dinero.
PUBLICIDAD
En este aspecto, Anthropic presenta un dato favorable. Un análisis realizado por Aleh Tsyvinski, profesor de Economía de Yale, encontró que el 22,5 % de los usuarios de Anthropic continuaba utilizando sus modelos 12 meses después de su primer uso. En OpenAI, la proporción era de aproximadamente 13,2 %.
Al mismo tiempo, el uso general de modelos de IA continúa creciendo. Los datos de OpenRouter muestran que el consumo de tokens, las unidades utilizadas para procesar las consultas, se multiplicó por 250 desde comienzos de 2025. Este aumento sustenta las expectativas de que el mercado todavía tenga espacio para expandirse.
PUBLICIDAD
El coste de desarrollar modelos cada vez más avanzados
Los inversores también deben valorar cuánto cuesta mantener este ritmo de innovación. Anthropic ha informado a sus inversores de que espera registrar un beneficio operativo ajustado por segundo trimestre consecutivo, mientras sus ingresos del segundo trimestre aumentaron hasta 11.500 millones de dólares y sus ingresos anualizados alcanzaron los 65.000 millones de dólares en julio.
Sin embargo, la compañía necesita realizar grandes inversiones para entrenar modelos cada vez más capaces. Su CEO, Dario Amodei, ha pedido recientemente que los laboratorios reduzcan el ritmo de desarrollo de los sistemas de vanguardia para mejorar la seguridad.
Una ralentización podría reducir los costes de entrenamiento de Anthropic, pero también daría más tiempo a competidores estadounidenses y chinos para acercarse tecnológicamente, una tensión que los inversores deberán valorar.
PUBLICIDAD
El riesgo de que la IA se convierta en un producto básico
La incertidumbre también se extiende al modelo de negocio de los laboratorios de IA. Ejecutivos tecnológicos han advertido que, a medida que aumente la competencia, los modelos podrían convertirse en servicios cada vez más intercambiables y baratos.
Esto supondría un desafío para empresas como Anthropic, que necesitan justificar valoraciones de cientos de miles de millones de dólares mediante un crecimiento sostenido y márgenes suficientes para compensar sus elevados costes de computación.
A estas dudas se suman la concentración de los ingresos entre grandes clientes y socios de infraestructura, posibles intervenciones gubernamentales y los riesgos sociales asociados con el desarrollo de sistemas de IA más avanzados.
PUBLICIDAD
Por ahora, Anthropic mantiene un crecimiento excepcional y ha comunicado señales de mejora en su rentabilidad. Pero la cuestión que deberán responder los mercados cuando la compañía salga a bolsa será si ese crecimiento puede mantenerse cuando la competencia sea mayor, los precios bajen y el desarrollo de modelos avanzados exija inversiones cada vez más elevadas.

articles.title: Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
articles.text:
Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
A breakthrough nanolaser could let future computer chips communicate with light, potentially doubling down on speed while cutting energy use in half.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- Technical University of Denmark
- Summary:
- Scientists have created an ultra-small nanolaser that could eventually allow microchips to transmit information with light instead of electricity, potentially making computers faster while cutting energy use roughly in half. Thousands of the lasers could fit on a single chip, opening possibilities for more efficient data centers, smartphones, and advanced medical sensors.
- Share:
The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.
In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.
"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.
Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.
Using Light Inside Computer Chips
Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.
Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.
Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.
The compact DTU nanolaser is an important step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.
Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers
The new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.
At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.
When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.
The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.
Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use
The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.
Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.
In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.
Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Technical University of Denmark. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Meng Xiong, Yi Yu, Yury Berdnikov, Simon Klinck Borregaard, Adrian Holm Dubré, Elizaveta Semenova, Kresten Yvind, Jesper Mørk. A nanolaser with extreme dielectric confinement. Science Advances, 2025; 11 (51) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adx3865
